text: In September 1928, a Scottish scientist named Alexander Fleming came back to his laboratory in London after a holiday. Before he left, he had been growing bacteria in small dishes. Now he started to clean them up, but one dish looked strange.

The dish was covered with bacteria, but there was also a spot of blue-green mould, a kind of fungus that grows on old food. Around the mould there was a clear ring where the bacteria were gone. It seemed that the mould was killing them. Perhaps the mould came through an open window, or from another room in the building. Nobody is sure.

Fleming did not throw the dish away. He grew more of the mould and tested it on other bacteria. Many kinds of dangerous bacteria were killed by it. He called the active substance in the mould 'penicillin'. He published his findings in 1929.

However, penicillin was hard to make in large amounts, and Fleming did not turn it into a medicine. That work was done in the late 1930s and 1940s by a team of scientists in Oxford, led by Howard Florey and Ernst Chain. Penicillin soon began to save the lives of soldiers and many other patients. In 1945, Fleming, Florey and Chain shared the Nobel Prize.

text: In September 1928, Alexander Fleming, a Scottish bacteriologist working at St Mary's Hospital in London, returned from a summer holiday to a cluttered laboratory. Before leaving, he had left several culture dishes of Staphylococcus, a common cause of infections, stacked on a bench. As he sorted through them, one dish caught his attention.

A spot of blue-green mould had contaminated the dish, and around it, the bacterial colonies had disappeared, leaving a clear ring. Fleming guessed that something produced by the mould was dissolving or killing the bacteria. How the mould had reached the dish is uncertain; the spores may have drifted in through an open window or up from a laboratory elsewhere in the building.

Rather than discarding the contaminated dish, Fleming investigated. He grew the mould, later identified as a species of Penicillium, in broth and found that the liquid it produced was able to stop the growth of many harmful bacteria, even when it was greatly diluted. He named the active substance 'penicillin' and published his results in 1929.

Yet the discovery did not change medicine immediately. Penicillin proved difficult to extract and unstable, and Fleming, who saw it mainly as a useful antiseptic and a laboratory tool, never succeeded in turning it into a reliable treatment. That task was taken up in Oxford at the end of the 1930s by Howard Florey, Ernst Chain and their colleagues, who developed methods of purifying and producing it in larger quantities. During the Second World War, penicillin was produced on an industrial scale and saved the lives of many wounded soldiers. In 1945, Fleming, Florey and Chain were jointly awarded the Nobel Prize. The story also changed how scientists thought about the natural world: moulds and bacteria are locked in a constant chemical competition, and substances produced in that competition can be turned into weapons against disease. Later, however, the overuse of antibiotics led to the spread of resistant bacteria, a danger that Fleming himself warned about in his Nobel lecture.

text: The discovery of penicillin is often told as a story of luck, yet luck alone does not explain it. As he sorted through them, one dish caught his attention.

A spot of blue-green mould had contaminated the dish, and around it, the bacterial colonies had disappeared, leaving a clear ring. Fleming inferred that something produced by the mould was dissolving or killing the bacteria. How the contamination occurred is uncertain; the spores may have drifted in through an open window or up from a laboratory elsewhere in the building. What mattered was that Fleming, who had spent years searching for substances that could combat infection, recognised the significance of what many others might have thrown away. He had, after all, discovered lysozyme in 1921, an enzyme found in tears and saliva that destroys some bacteria, so he was prepared to take such an observation seriously.

He grew the mould, later identified as a species of Penicillium, in broth and found that the liquid it produced could inhibit the growth of many harmful bacteria, even when greatly diluted. He named the active substance 'penicillin' and published his findings in 1929. The paper attracted limited attention, partly because penicillin proved difficult to extract and unstable, and Fleming, who regarded it mainly as a topical antiseptic and a laboratory tool, never succeeded in developing it into a dependable therapy.

That achievement belongs largely to a team in Oxford, where, at the end of the 1930s, Howard Florey, Ernst Chain and their colleagues developed methods of purifying penicillin and producing it in useful quantities. The urgency of the Second World War then accelerated industrial production, and the drug saved many wounded soldiers. In 1945, Fleming, Florey and Chain shared the Nobel Prize, a reminder that a discovery and its development are often the work of different people, and that a promising observation can wait for years until someone finds a way to make use of it. The story also changed how scientists thought about the natural world: moulds and bacteria are locked in a constant chemical competition, and substances produced in that competition can be turned into weapons against disease. Later, however, the overuse of antibiotics led to the spread of resistant bacteria, a danger that Fleming himself warned about in his Nobel lecture.

text: In the 1700s, smallpox was one of the most dangerous diseases in the world. Many people died, and those who lived often had scars on their faces for the rest of their lives. In English villages, people noticed something strange. Women who milked cows often caught a mild disease from the animals, called cowpox. These women usually did not get smallpox.

A country doctor named Edward Jenner wanted to find out if this was true. In 1796, he took a little liquid from a cowpox sore on the hand of a milkmaid, Sarah Nelmes. He put it into small cuts on the arm of a healthy eight-year-old boy, James Phipps. The boy felt a little ill for a few days, but he got better.
A few weeks later, Jenner did the most important part of his test. He gave the boy a small amount of real smallpox. The boy did not get the disease. The cowpox had protected him.

Jenner wrote about his results in 1798. He called the new method 'vaccination', from the Latin word for cow. Today we know that such an experiment would not be allowed, because it was dangerous for the boy. But Jenner's idea saved millions of lives. In 1980, the World Health Organization announced that smallpox had disappeared from the world.

text: By the eighteenth century, smallpox had become one of the most feared diseases in Europe. It killed roughly one in three of those it infected, and survivors were often left blind or disfigured. Some people tried a risky form of protection, called variolation, which meant deliberately infecting a healthy person with material from a mild case; it often worked, but it could also cause a deadly infection and spread the disease to others.

In the English countryside, a rumour had long circulated that milkmaids were rarely disfigured by smallpox. Edward Jenner, a doctor in Gloucestershire, took the rumour seriously. text: Smallpox was among the most feared diseases of the eighteenth century. It killed roughly one in three of those it infected, and survivors were frequently left blind or permanently scarred. A risky practice known as variolation, in which healthy people were deliberately infected with material from a mild case, offered some protection, but it could itself prove fatal and could spread the disease to others. The practice had reached Britain from the Ottoman Empire early in the century, popularised by Lady Mary Wortley Montagu, who had observed it in Constantinople.

Against this background, a piece of rural folklore acquired unexpected significance. It was widely said in the English countryside that milkmaids, who often contracted cowpox, a mild illness that produced sores on the hands, escaped the ravages of smallpox. Edward Jenner, a physician practising in Gloucestershire, took the claim seriously and suspected that the earlier infection conferred some kind of immunity.

In May 1796, he put the idea to the test. He took material from a cowpox sore on the hand of a milkmaid, Sarah Nelmes, and introduced it into small incisions in the arm of James Phipps, an eight-year-old boy. Phipps developed a mild fever and recovered promptly. Several weeks later, Jenner exposed the boy to material from a smallpox sore, and no disease followed, which strongly suggested that the cowpox had given him lasting protection.

Jenner published his findings in 1798 and coined the term 'vaccination' from the Latin word for cow. By modern standards, the experiment was ethically indefensible, since a child had been knowingly exposed to a lethal disease, and Jenner was not the first to notice the connection: a farmer named Benjamin Jesty is reported to have inoculated his own family with cowpox some twenty years earlier. What distinguished Jenner was the care with which he recorded his observations and the persistence with which he promoted the method.

His first report had been turned down by the Royal Society, which wanted more evidence, and some critics objected on religious grounds, while others feared that material from cows would have unpredictable effects on the human body. Resistance was considerable, yet the evidence accumulated, and vaccination spread across Europe and beyond. Nearly two centuries later, a global campaign coordinated by the World Health Organization led to the declaration, in 1980, that smallpox had been eradicated, the first human disease to be eliminated in this way.

text: In the 1700s, sailors on long sea trips often got a terrible disease called scurvy. Their gums bled, their teeth fell out, and their old wounds opened again. Thousands of sailors died. Nobody knew the cause, and people tried many different cures.

All of them ate the same basic food. But each pair also received a different treatment. One pair drank cider. One pair took a medicine with acid in it. One pair drank vinegar. After about a week, the result was clear. The two sailors who ate oranges and a lemon got better very fast. One of them was ready to work again, and the other helped to look after the sick men. The other pairs improved little or not at all.

text: Scurvy was one of the great killers of the age of sail. On long voyages, sailors developed swollen and bleeding gums, extreme weakness, and wounds that had healed long before opened again. By some estimates, the disease killed more British sailors in the eighteenth century than enemy action did. On Commodore George Anson's famous voyage around the world in the 1740s, most of the crew who died succumbed to scurvy rather than to battle. Remedies abounded, but nobody had tested them systematically.

This is what James Lind, a Scottish naval surgeon, set out to do in 1747. Aboard HMS Salisbury, he selected twelve men whose symptoms were as similar as possible and divided them into six pairs. All twelve received the same basic diet, but each pair was given a different supposed cure: cider, a dilute acid solution, vinegar, sea water, a paste of spices, or two oranges and a lemon a day.

The two sailors who had received the oranges and the lemon recovered rapidly: within about a week, one was fit for duty again and the other was well enough to nurse the remaining patients. The other pairs showed little or no improvement, although the men who had drunk cider fared slightly better than the rest.

Lind's experiment is now regarded as an early example of a controlled trial, since it compared treatments under similar conditions. Yet its impact was surprisingly limited. Lind published a detailed account of the trial in 1753, but it appeared inside a long treatise in which the experiment occupied only a few pages, so many readers may simply have overlooked it. Lind himself did not fully trust his own result, partly because he continued to believe that damp air also played a part, and the supply of fresh fruit on ships was difficult and expensive to maintain. It was not until the 1790s that the navy began to issue lemon juice to its crews as a regular ration. The real reason for its effectiveness, the vitamin C it contains, was understood only in the twentieth century.

text: For much of the age of sail, scurvy was the scourge of long-distance seafaring. Its symptoms, which included swollen and bleeding gums, extreme exhaustion, and the reopening of long-healed wounds, could incapacitate entire crews, and by some estimates the disease claimed more British naval lives in the eighteenth century than enemy action did. On Commodore George Anson's famous voyage around the world in the 1740s, most of the crew who died succumbed to scurvy rather than to battle. Remedies abounded, but they rested largely on tradition and speculation rather than on systematic comparison.

It was this gap that James Lind, a Scottish naval surgeon, set out to fill in 1747. Aboard HMS Salisbury, he selected twelve men whose symptoms appeared as similar as possible, housed them together, and fed them an identical basic diet. He then divided them into six pairs, each of which received a different supposed cure: cider, a dilute acid solution, vinegar, sea water, a paste of spices, or two oranges and a lemon each day.

The two sailors who had received the citrus fruit recovered with striking speed: within roughly a week, one was fit for duty again and the other was well enough to nurse the remaining patients. The other pairs showed little or no improvement, though the cider drinkers fared slightly better than the rest. Because Lind had compared treatments under conditions that were as uniform as he could make them, his trial is often described as an early example of a controlled clinical experiment.

What is remarkable, however, is how slowly the lesson was applied. Lind's own conclusions were hedged: he continued to believe that damp air contributed to scurvy, and he doubted whether fresh fruit could be supplied to ships on a large scale. His results attracted little attention for decades, and it was not until the 1790s that the navy introduced lemon juice as a regular ration. The reason for its effectiveness, a dietary deficiency of vitamin C, was understood only in the twentieth century, which suggests that a result can be demonstrated long before it can be explained, and longer still before it is acted upon. The episode is frequently invoked to illustrate how medical knowledge advances: not in a single decisive moment, but through a slow process of testing, doubt, and institutional inertia, in which even a well-designed experiment may be overlooked for years.

text: Few episodes in the history of medicine illustrate so painfully how evidence can fail to persuade. In the 1840s, the Vienna General Hospital operated two maternity clinics that admitted patients in turn. Ignaz Semmelweis, a Hungarian physician appointed assistant in the First Clinic in 1846, was troubled by this gap. He methodically ruled out the explanations then in vogue, including overcrowding, ventilation, and the posture adopted during labour, since none of them could account for a difference between two institutions exposed to virtually identical conditions. What distinguished his approach was its reliance on figures: he compared mortality between the two clinics month by month, and the disparity persisted with remarkable consistency.

The breakthrough came, tragically, through a death. In 1847, his colleague Jakob Kolletschka died after being cut with a scalpel during an autopsy, and Semmelweis recognised in the post-mortem findings a pathology strikingly similar to that of the women dying on his ward. The inference was uncomfortable: the doctors and students who handled corpses in the morning and examined women in labour afterwards were themselves the vector of the disease, whereas the midwives, who performed no autopsies, were not. Semmelweis attributed the contagion to 'cadaverous particles', a notion that predated the germ theory by years.

His remedy was disarmingly simple. He required everyone to wash their hands in a chlorinated lime solution before examining patients, and mortality in the First Clinic fell dramatically, in some months approaching that of the midwives' clinic.

Yet the evidence alone was not enough. Semmelweis offered no explanation that fitted prevailing medical doctrine; his conclusion implied that physicians had unwittingly killed their own patients, a suggestion many found intolerable; and his reluctance to publish promptly, together with an increasingly confrontational temperament, did little to win over sceptics. He died in 1865, his work largely dismissed. It was only after Pasteur and Lister had established the role of microorganisms that his contribution was recognised, and he is now regarded as a pioneer of antisepsis, though historians continue to debate how much of the opposition was scientific and how much personal.

text: Smallpox was among the most feared diseases in human history. It caused a high fever and a rash of painful blisters, and about three in ten of those infected died. The early strategy was mass vaccination, with the aim of immunising about eighty per cent of every population. This worked in some countries, but it proved impractical in regions with poor roads, civil war and shortages of vaccine. The team directed by the American epidemiologist Donald Henderson therefore adopted a more targeted strategy, known as surveillance and containment. Teams searched for every new case, isolated the patient and vaccinated everyone in the surrounding community, so that the virus ran out of people to infect. Because smallpox has no animal reservoir, and because it is usually obvious who is ill, the approach was particularly effective. The programme also benefited from a cheap, two-pronged needle that could be used by workers with minimal training.

The last natural case occurred in Somalia in October 1977, in a hospital cook named Ali Maow Maalin, who recovered. On 8 May 1980, the WHO declared smallpox eradicated, the only human disease ever to have been eliminated. Stocks of the virus are still kept in two high-security laboratories, and scientists continue to debate whether they should be destroyed, since they might be useful for research while posing a risk if they escaped.

text: In 1854, a terrible disease called cholera hit the Soho area of London. In a few weeks, hundreds of people died. At that time, most doctors believed that the disease came from bad air. They called it 'miasma', a poisonous mist from dirty places.

A doctor named John Snow did not agree. He thought that cholera came from dirty water. To test his idea, he visited the houses of the sick people and asked where they got their water. Then he drew a map and marked every death on it.
The map showed something clear. Most of the deaths were near a water pump on Broad Street. People who lived closer to other pumps got sick much less often.

Snow also found some interesting exceptions. Workers at a nearby brewery seemed to stay healthy. They had their own well, and they often drank beer instead of water. A woman who lived far away in Hampstead died after she drank water from the Broad Street pump. She liked its taste, so her family sent it to her in bottles.

Snow told the local officials about his findings. They removed the handle of the pump, so people could not use it any more. The number of new cases was already falling by then, so we cannot be sure how much the change helped. But Snow's map showed a new way to find the cause of a disease, and doctors still use this idea today.

text: At the time, most doctors believed that cholera was spread through 'miasma', a poisonous mist thought to rise from rotting waste and fill the air of crowded districts. John Snow, a London physician, was not convinced. He had already suggested that cholera was carried by contaminated water, but few of his colleagues took the idea seriously, since the available evidence could be explained in other ways.

When the outbreak began in Soho in late August 1854, Snow went from door to door, asking families where the victims had lived and what they had drunk. He marked each death on a map of the area. The pattern was striking: the deaths clustered around a public water pump on Broad Street, while houses closer to other pumps had far fewer cases.

Snow also paid attention to the exceptions, which proved just as informative. A nearby workhouse, which had its own well, recorded very few deaths among its several hundred residents. Workers at a local brewery also seemed to escape the disease, as they rarely used the pump. Conversely, a woman who lived far away in Hampstead died after having bottles of water from the Broad Street pump delivered to her, because she preferred its taste.

On 7 September, Snow presented his findings to the local authorities. They were sceptical, but agreed, as a precaution, to remove the handle of the pump so that nobody could draw water from it. Interestingly, the number of new cases was already falling by then, perhaps because many residents had left the area, so the removal of the handle alone cannot be said to have ended the outbreak.

Nevertheless, Snow's map convinced a growing number of people that disease could be traced to a specific source. A later investigation by a local clergyman, Henry Whitehead, who had initially doubted Snow's theory, found a cesspit close to the pump's well that had been leaking, and linked it to a household where an infant had fallen ill just before the outbreak. The bacterium that causes cholera was not identified conclusively until decades later, yet Snow's method of mapping cases and asking where they differed became one of the foundations of modern epidemiology.

text: The 1854 cholera outbreak in London's Soho district is often cited as the founding episode of modern epidemiology, yet the story is more nuanced than the legend suggests. At the time, the prevailing explanation for cholera was the miasma theory, according to which the disease was spread by foul air rising from decaying matter. John Snow, a London physician who had already proposed that cholera was transmitted through contaminated water, found little support among his colleagues, partly because his hypothesis lacked decisive proof.

When the outbreak erupted in late August, Snow set about collecting evidence systematically. He interviewed bereaved households, established where each victim had obtained drinking water, and plotted the deaths on a map. The resulting pattern pointed unmistakably to a public pump on Broad Street, around which the cases were densely concentrated.

More persuasive still were the anomalies. A workhouse in the area, which drew water from its own well, recorded remarkably few deaths among several hundred inmates, and workers at a nearby brewery seemed largely to escape infection. Conversely, a woman living in Hampstead, far from the epidemic, died after having water from the Broad Street pump delivered to her, a detail Snow considered particularly telling.

Snow presented his findings to the local board of guardians on 7 September, and the pump handle was removed shortly afterwards. The effect of this measure is difficult to judge: the outbreak had already begun to subside, possibly because many residents had fled, so the removal of the handle cannot be credited with ending the epidemic. Even so, the authorities' own report remained unconvinced, and it was not until a later investigation by the clergyman Henry Whitehead, initially a sceptic, identified a likely source of contamination, a leaking cesspit close to the well, that Snow's reasoning gained wider credibility.

The bacterium responsible was not identified conclusively until decades later, but Snow's method, which consisted of mapping cases and examining where the pattern broke down, endured. It remains a model of how disciplined observation can reveal a cause long before the underlying mechanism is understood. Its limits are worth noting, however: Snow could demonstrate an association between the pump and the deaths, but the way in which water carried the disease remained a matter of inference rather than observation. In that sense, the episode illustrates both the power and the limits of purely statistical reasoning in medicine.

text: For a long time, nobody knew why the dinosaurs disappeared about sixty-six million years ago. Some scientists thought the climate changed slowly. Others suggested diseases or volcanoes. In the 1970s, a geologist named Walter Alvarez studied rocks near the town of Gubbio, in Italy. In the rock layers, he found a thin band of clay. Below the clay there were many tiny sea animals. Above it there were far fewer. The clay seemed to mark the moment when many species disappeared.

Walter asked his father, Luis Alvarez, a famous physicist, to help him find out how long this clay layer took to form. They tested it for a very rare metal called iridium. Iridium is almost never found in rocks on the surface of the Earth, but it is common in asteroids. To their surprise, the clay contained much more iridium than normal rock.

The Alvarez team suggested that a huge asteroid, perhaps ten kilometres wide, hit the Earth. The impact would have thrown dust into the air and darkened the sky for months. Plants would have died, and the animals that ate them would have followed. They published their idea in 1980.

Many scientists did not believe it at first, because there was no crater. Then, in the 1990s, researchers confirmed a giant crater buried under Mexico's Yucatán coast, called Chicxulub. It was the right age. Today, most scientists accept that an asteroid impact played a major part in the end of the dinosaurs, although some think that volcanoes also contributed.
versions.proof: To their surprise, the clay contained much more iridium than normal rock.

text: For more than a century, the disappearance of the dinosaurs about sixty-six million years ago was one of the great puzzles of science. Explanations ranged from slow climate change to disease, and from changes in sea level to volcanic activity. None was supported by strong evidence, and most scientists assumed that the extinction had been gradual.

In the 1970s, the geologist Walter Alvarez studied a layer of clay in the rocks near Gubbio, in Italy, which marked the boundary between two geological periods. Below the clay, the rocks contained many microscopic marine fossils; above it, there were very few. The clay layer, in other words, seemed to record the moment when large numbers of species vanished. Alvarez wanted to know how long the clay had taken to accumulate, and he asked his father, the Nobel Prize-winning physicist Luis Alvarez, for help.

The two decided to measure the amount of iridium in the clay. Iridium is extremely rare in the Earth's crust, but it is more abundant in meteorites, so its quantity can serve as a kind of clock for the fall of cosmic dust. To their surprise, the layer contained far more iridium than they had expected, and similar layers elsewhere in the world showed the same pattern. Together with two colleagues, they proposed in 1980 that an asteroid roughly ten kilometres wide had struck the Earth. The impact would have thrown enormous amounts of dust into the atmosphere, blocking sunlight, disrupting photosynthesis, and causing food chains to collapse.

The hypothesis was met with scepticism, partly because no crater had been found. The breakthrough came in the early 1990s, when scientists identified a buried crater about 180 kilometres across, called Chicxulub, beneath the Yucatán Peninsula in Mexico. Its age matched the extinction. Today most researchers accept that an impact was a major cause of the mass extinction, though some argue that massive volcanic eruptions in India also played a part, and debate continues about how the two events interacted.

The impact, they argued, would have thrown enormous amounts of dust into the atmosphere, blocking sunlight, disrupting photosynthesis, and causing food chains to collapse.

text: High above the Earth, there is a thin layer of gas called ozone. It acts like a sunscreen for the planet, because it blocks much of the dangerous ultraviolet light from the sun. Without it, more people would get skin cancer, and plants and sea animals would suffer.

In 1974, two chemists, Mario Molina and Sherwood Rowland, warned that some man-made gases might destroy ozone. These gases were called CFCs, and they were used in fridges, air conditioners and spray cans. At first, many people and some companies did not take the warning seriously.

In 1985, a group of British scientists working in Antarctica reported something shocking. Each spring, the ozone layer above the continent was much thinner than before. Newspapers soon called it the 'ozone hole'. Satellite pictures confirmed the discovery, and the evidence that CFCs were the cause became very strong.

The world reacted quickly. In 1987, countries signed an agreement called the Montreal Protocol, promising to stop making CFCs. Companies found safer gases to use instead. The agreement worked. Today the ozone layer is slowly recovering, and scientists expect it to return to its earlier state in a few decades. Many people consider this agreement a rare example of countries working together to solve a global problem.

text: The ozone layer, a thin region of the upper atmosphere, absorbs most of the sun's harmful ultraviolet radiation. Without it, rates of skin cancer and eye disease would rise sharply, and the crops and plankton on which food chains depend would be damaged. In 1974, the chemists Mario Molina and Sherwood Rowland warned that chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs), widely used in refrigerators, air conditioners and aerosol cans, could rise into the stratosphere and destroy ozone there. Their claim was disputed by some industries, which pointed out that the evidence was largely theoretical.

The theory was dramatically confirmed in 1985, when Joseph Farman, Brian Gardiner and Jonathan Shanklin of the British Antarctic Survey reported that the spring ozone levels above Antarctica had fallen sharply since the 1970s. The phenomenon, which was quickly named the 'ozone hole', had been missed by earlier satellite measurements because the computer programs used to analyse the data had treated unusually low readings as errors. Once scientists went back and examined the raw data, the problem was obvious, and laboratory and field studies soon established that chlorine from CFCs was responsible.

The international response was unusually swift. In 1987, governments signed the Montreal Protocol, which committed them to phase out ozone-damaging substances, and it was later strengthened several times. Industry developed substitutes, and the agreement is often described as the most successful environmental treaty ever made. Measurements now show that the ozone layer is gradually recovering, and scientists expect it to return to levels seen before 1980 around the middle of the century. The case is often used as evidence that, when scientists provide clear evidence and governments act together, global environmental problems can be solved. It also shows how much a single research station, with a handful of patient observers, can change the course of world politics.

It is a reminder that automated analysis can conceal precisely the anomalies that matter most.

Several factors helped: the scientific evidence was clear, the risks were easy for the public to understand, and chemical companies, once they had developed profitable substitutes, no longer had a strong reason to resist. Molina, Rowland and the atmospheric chemist Paul Crutzen shared the 1995 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for their work.

text: For hundreds of years, many people believed in 'spontaneous generation'. This was the idea that small living things could appear from nothing. text: Until the middle of the nineteenth century, many educated people accepted the doctrine of spontaneous generation, the belief that living organisms could arise directly from non-living matter. Maggots seemed to appear in rotting meat, and microscopic organisms seemed to appear in broth that had been left standing. Louis Pasteur, who suspected that Pouchet's flasks had been contaminated, designed a more careful test. He boiled a nutrient broth in flasks whose necks he had drawn out into long, S-shaped curves. Air could pass freely through the neck, but dust particles and the microbes attached to them were trapped on the bends.

The broth remained clear for months, even though it was in constant contact with the air. When Pasteur tilted a flask so that the broth touched the trapped dust, or broke off the neck altogether, microbes appeared within a day or two. The experiment showed that microbes were already present in the air and settled on food; they did not arise from the broth itself. The experiment had a number of practical consequences. It supported the germ theory of disease, encouraged the use of sterile methods in surgery, and led to pasteurisation, a method of heating liquids to reduce the number of microbes. text: The Piltdown skull was announced in December 1912 by Charles Dawson, a lawyer and enthusiastic amateur archaeologist, together with Arthur Smith Woodward of the British Museum. Dawson claimed to have found fragments of a skull and jaw in a gravel pit in East Sussex. The skull was large and rounded like that of a modern human, but the jaw resembled an ape's. This combination fitted a popular theory of the time, which held that a large brain had evolved first, and the find was welcomed as the 'missing link' between apes and humans. It was also a source of national pride, since Britain had no famous early human fossils to rival those found in Germany and France.

Doubts accumulated slowly. From the 1920s, discoveries in Africa and Asia suggested that human ancestors had developed upright walking before large brains, which meant that Piltdown Man did not fit the emerging picture. Even so, it remained in textbooks for decades, partly because the museum that held the bones allowed few researchers to examine them.

The truth emerged in 1953, when a team including Joseph Weiner, Kenneth Oakley and Wilfrid Le Gros Clark subjected the specimens to modern tests. Fluorine analysis showed that the skull was far younger than the gravel in which it had been 'found', and microscopic study revealed that the teeth had been filed down to resemble human wear. The bones had also been stained with chemicals to give them an ancient appearance. The skull belonged to a modern human, and the jaw to an orangutan.

Who carried out the forgery has never been settled. Dawson is the most common suspect, but other names have been proposed, and the evidence remains circumstantial. What the episode demonstrates is how easily expectations can influence scientific judgement: the fraud succeeded not only because it was skilful, but also because it told researchers what they wished to hear.

This combination matched a prevailing theory that the human brain had expanded before other features, and the find was welcomed as the long-sought 'missing link'. Doubts accumulated slowly. From the 1920s, discoveries in Africa and Asia suggested that our ancestors had walked upright long before their brains grew large, a pattern that Piltdown Man contradicted. Yet the specimen survived in textbooks for decades, partly because access to the original bones was tightly controlled, and partly because many experts preferred to treat the fossil as an anomaly rather than as a challenge to their expectations.

Who perpetrated the forgery has never been settled. Dawson is the most frequent suspect, but other names have been proposed, and the evidence remains circumstantial. What is clearer is why the deception worked: it was skilful enough to pass casual inspection, but, more importantly, it told researchers what they already wished to believe. The episode is therefore remembered less as a story of one forger than as a warning about confirmation bias, and about the value of allowing independent scientists to examine the evidence for themselves. text: In December 1952, London was very cold. Most people heated their homes with coal, so every chimney in the city sent smoke into the air. Factories and power stations also burned a lot of coal. text: In early December 1952, London experienced a spell of unusually cold weather, and Londoners burned more coal than usual to keep warm. The coal available to ordinary households at the time was often of poor quality, and it produced large amounts of sulphur-rich smoke. On 5 December, an anticyclone settled over the Thames Valley, and a layer of warm air trapped the cold air beneath it. This phenomenon, known as a temperature inversion, prevented the smoke from rising, and with no wind to disperse it, the pollution mixed with fog and thickened into a dense, yellowish haze.

The Great Smog, as it came to be known, lasted for about four days. Visibility fell to a few metres in places, public transport was disrupted, and the ambulance service was reduced to carrying patients in whatever vehicles could move. Yet many Londoners were slow to appreciate the danger, since heavy fogs, known as 'pea-soupers', were a familiar feature of the city.

The medical consequences became apparent only afterwards. Hospitals admitted large numbers of patients with breathing difficulties, and undertakers ran out of coffins. The official estimate was about four thousand deaths, but later research, which compared death rates with those in normal weeks, suggested that the true figure was probably between ten and twelve thousand. Those most affected were infants, the elderly, and people with chronic heart or lung disease.

The disaster is widely regarded as a turning point. Public pressure eventually led to the Clean Air Act of 1956, which introduced smoke-control areas where households were not allowed to burn coal in open fires, and encouraged the use of smokeless fuels and electricity. Subsequent decades saw a steady improvement in the capital's air. The episode remains an important example in discussions of public health and environmental policy, because it showed that air pollution was not a mere inconvenience, but a cause of mass death.

text: At about seven o'clock on the morning of 30 June 1908, a brilliant fireball crossed the sky above a remote region of central Siberia and exploded with a force that was felt hundreds of kilometres away. Witnesses described a column of light, followed by a series of thunderous noises, and windows were broken in settlements far from the site. For several nights afterwards, the skies over Europe and Asia glowed so brightly that, according to some accounts, people could read newspapers outdoors at midnight.

Because of the remoteness of the area and the political upheavals of the period, the first scientific expedition did not reach it until 1927, led by the Russian mineralogist Leonid Kulik. He expected to find a huge crater, the sign of a giant meteorite. What he found instead was a vast area of devastated forest. Roughly eighty million trees, spread over some two thousand square kilometres, lay flattened in a radial pattern pointing away from the centre, while the trees at the centre itself were stripped of their branches but still standing. There was no crater.

This unusual pattern is now explained by what is called an airburst. According to the most widely accepted theory, a stony asteroid, perhaps fifty metres wide, entered the atmosphere at great speed and exploded several kilometres above the ground. The shock wave from the explosion, whose energy has been estimated at about ten to fifteen million tonnes of TNT, flattened the trees without leaving a crater, since the object had broken apart before it hit the surface.

A number of more exotic explanations, including antimatter and alien spacecraft, have been put forward, but none is supported by evidence. The event is taken seriously by astronomers for a practical reason: if a similar object exploded above a densely populated area, the consequences would be catastrophic, which is one reason why scientists now search the sky for such objects.

text: In the third century BC, the Greek kings who ruled Egypt decided to build the greatest library in the world in their capital, Alexandria. Their aim was to collect all the books of all the peoples they knew. Scholars from many countries came to work there, and the library became part of a research centre called the Mouseion. Because books at that time were handwritten scrolls, nobody knows exactly how many were in the library. Modern estimates range from tens of thousands to several hundred thousand.

The rulers were very serious about collecting books. According to ancient writers, ships that arrived in the port were searched, and any scrolls on board were taken to the library and copied. The owners often received the copies, and the library kept the originals. The scholars worked on catalogues, corrected texts and made important discoveries. For example, Eratosthenes, who was the head of the library, calculated the size of the Earth with surprising accuracy.

Many people believe that the library was destroyed in a single great fire. In fact, the real story is much longer and more complicated. A fire during the war of Julius Caesar in 48 BC damaged part of the city, though how much of the library was lost is not clear. Later, the kings gave less money to the library, scholars were forced to leave in times of conflict, and the city suffered from wars and unrest. By the third and fourth centuries AD, the main library had probably disappeared, and a smaller library in a temple was destroyed in 391.
A popular story says that a Muslim caliph burned the library in the seventh century, but historians think that this is a legend, written long afterwards.

text: In the early third century BC, the Greek dynasty that ruled Egypt after Alexander the Great founded a library in its capital, Alexandria, with the ambitious aim of collecting all the world's books. Attached to a research institution known as the Mouseion, it attracted scholars from across the Mediterranean, who were given salaries and freedom to study. Because books were handwritten scrolls, the number it held is unknown, and modern estimates range from tens of thousands to several hundred thousand.

The Ptolemies pursued their goal with remarkable energy. According to ancient writers, ships that docked in the harbour were searched, and any scrolls they carried were confiscated, copied, and the copies returned to their owners, while the originals went to the library. The scholars established standard versions of Homer's poems, compiled a huge catalogue of the collection, and made discoveries in several sciences. Eratosthenes, who directed the library, calculated the circumference of the Earth with an error of only a small percentage.

Popular accounts tell of a single catastrophe, usually a fire, which destroyed the library overnight. The historical reality is less dramatic and more gradual. A fire during Julius Caesar's campaign in 48 BC damaged part of the city, but how much of the collection was lost is disputed. More lasting damage came from political decline: successive rulers cut funding, scholars were expelled during periods of conflict, and the city suffered from wars and civil unrest. By the third century AD, the main library had probably ceased to exist, and a smaller daughter library in a temple, the Serapeum, was destroyed in 391.

The well-known story that a Muslim caliph ordered the books burned in the seventh century appears only in sources written centuries later, and most historians regard it as a legend. The library's fate therefore teaches an uncomfortable lesson: great collections of knowledge are rarely destroyed by a single act; they fade when the societies that sustain them lose interest or resources.

text: The 1920s in the United States were called the Roaring Twenties. The economy grew fast, factories produced new cars, radios and refrigerators, and many people felt that they would soon be rich. Thousands of ordinary Americans started to buy shares in companies on Wall Street, the centre of the American stock market. Share prices went up and up, so buying shares seemed like an easy way to make money.

Many people bought shares with borrowed money. This is called buying on margin. An investor paid only a small part of the price and borrowed the rest from a broker. It worked well when prices were rising. But it was dangerous, because if the prices fell, the investor still had to pay back the loan.

In October 1929, prices began to fall. On 24 October, a day later called Black Thursday, panic started, and everybody tried to sell at the same time. Then, on 28 and 29 October, the market collapsed. Billions of dollars disappeared in a few days, and many people lost their savings.

Many people believe that the crash alone caused the Great Depression, the long economic crisis of the 1930s. But most historians say it was only one of the causes. In the following years, thousands of banks failed, and people lost their deposits. The government and the central bank made mistakes, and trade between countries fell. By 1933, around a quarter of American workers had no job. The crash was a warning sign and a trigger, but a weak economy and wrong decisions made the crisis much worse.
versions.proof: But most historians say it was only one of the causes.

text: The 1920s were a decade of exceptional prosperity in the United States. New industries, such as car manufacturing and electrical goods, expanded rapidly, and consumer credit made it possible for ordinary families to buy products they could not otherwise afford. The stock market became a national obsession, and by the late 1920s, millions of Americans were investing, many of them with money borrowed from brokers, a practice known as buying on margin. Investors needed to deposit only a fraction of the price of the shares, so a small fall in prices could wipe out their savings and force them to sell.

The first signs of weakness appeared in September 1929. On 24 October, known as Black Thursday, heavy selling began, and panic spread on 28 and 29 October, when the main index fell by about a fifth in two days. Billions of dollars of paper wealth disappeared, and many investors who had borrowed to buy shares were ruined. The market continued to fall, with brief recoveries, until 1932.

It is tempting to say that the crash caused the Great Depression, but most economists today would not accept so simple an explanation. The crash undoubtedly damaged confidence, and reduced the spending of wealthy households. However, the severity of the crisis in the following years had other causes. Thousands of banks failed in the early 1930s because they had too little cash to repay depositors, and the money supply shrank when the central bank, fearing inflation, refused to provide emergency loans. The Smoot-Hawley Tariff of 1930, which raised duties on thousands of imports, provoked retaliation from other countries and reduced world trade. By 1933, roughly a quarter of American workers were unemployed.

The crash is therefore best seen as a symptom and a trigger rather than the sole cause. The lessons of the 1930s led to the creation of deposit insurance, tighter regulation of banks and of the stock exchange, and a greater willingness of governments to intervene to protect the economy.
versions.proof: It is tempting to say that the crash caused the Great Depression, but most economists today would not accept so simple an explanation.

text: Johannes Gutenberg, a goldsmith from the German city of Mainz, is often credited with inventing printing around 1450. In reality, printing had a much longer history in East Asia. Woodblock printing was used in China from at least the ninth century, a Chinese craftsman named Bi Sheng experimented with movable type made of clay in the eleventh century, and in 1377 Korean printers produced a Buddhist text, the Jikji, with movable metal type. The reasons why these inventions did not transform society as quickly as Gutenberg's did are still debated; one explanation is that written Chinese uses thousands of different characters, which made movable type far less practical than an alphabet of a few dozen letters.

What Gutenberg achieved was to combine several technologies into an effective system. He devised a method of casting identical metal letters in large quantities, and he produced an oil-based ink that adhered to metal, unlike the water-based inks then in use. He also adapted a screw press, of the kind used for pressing wine and olives, to apply even pressure to the page. The result was that a workshop could produce many identical copies far more quickly and cheaply than a team of scribes.

His most famous book, the Gutenberg Bible, was completed around 1455, in an edition of about 180 copies. Despite the technical triumph, Gutenberg did not profit from it. He had borrowed heavily from a Mainz financier, Johann Fust, and when he failed to repay the debt, a court gave Fust ownership of much of the equipment.

Printing, however, spread rapidly through Europe. By 1500, presses were operating in more than two hundred towns, and it has been estimated that millions of volumes had been printed. The cost of books fell sharply, literacy slowly increased, and scientific, religious and political ideas circulated with a speed that was without precedent. Historians disagree about how far the press itself caused later events such as the Reformation, but few doubt that it changed the way knowledge was shared.

His training as a metalworker was essential, since the precision of the type determined the quality of the printed page.

He had borrowed heavily from a Mainz financier, Johann Fust, and when he failed to repay the debt, a court gave Fust ownership of much of the equipment. Many details of his life, including his year of birth, remain uncertain, since he left few documents behind and did not even put his name on his books.

Historians disagree about how far the press itself caused later events such as the Reformation, since reformers also needed readers, audiences and political protection, but few doubt that it changed the way knowledge was shared.

The story of Gutenberg is therefore a good example of how innovation works in practice. It is rarely a matter of a lone genius inventing something from nothing; more often, it consists of putting existing ideas together in the right place, at the right moment, and in a form that others can copy.

text: In 1961, a psychologist at Yale University named Stanley Milgram started a famous experiment. He wanted to understand why so many ordinary people obeyed cruel orders during the Second World War. Would normal people do something terrible if an authority told them to?

The learner sat in another room and had to remember word pairs. Each time he made a mistake, the teacher had to press a switch to give him an electric shock. The shocks got stronger every time, from 15 volts up to 450 volts. In fact, there were no real shocks, but the teachers did not know this.

As the shocks got stronger, the learner shouted, complained, and finally became silent. Many teachers were very nervous. They sweated, shook, and asked to stop. But a man in a grey coat, who was the experimenter, calmly told them to continue. 'The experiment requires that you go on.'

Before the experiment, Milgram asked other people how many volunteers would continue to the highest level. They said very few, maybe one in a hundred. But the result was a shock: about two thirds of the volunteers in the first version gave the highest shock. The experiment suggested that situations and authority can influence people more than we expect. However, many people criticised the study, because the volunteers suffered a lot of stress.

text: In 1961, shortly after the trial of the Nazi official Adolf Eichmann had begun in Jerusalem, the Yale psychologist Stanley Milgram started a series of experiments to investigate a troubling question: could ordinary people be induced to harm an innocent person simply because an authority figure told them to? Many people believed that such behaviour was limited to unusually cruel individuals or to particular cultures, and that most Americans would refuse.

Volunteers were recruited through newspaper advertisements and told they were taking part in a study of memory and learning. The experiments are often interpreted as showing the power of authority and of the situation, but they have also been criticised. text: For more than a thousand years, nobody could read the writing of ancient Egypt. The beautiful picture-signs on temples and tombs, called hieroglyphs, were a mystery. Scholars guessed that each sign was a picture of an idea, but they could not prove it, and no one could say what the texts really said.

In 1799, French soldiers who were building a fort near the town of Rosetta, in Egypt, found a large dark stone. It was covered with writing in three different styles. The top part had Egyptian hieroglyphs. The middle part was a simpler Egyptian script, called Demotic. The bottom part was in Greek. Scholars could read Greek easily, and they soon understood that the three parts probably said the same thing. This meant that the Greek could be a key to the other two.

After the French lost to the British army in Egypt, the stone was given to Britain, and it has been in the British Museum in London since 1802. Copies were made, and scholars in many countries tried to read the hieroglyphs. An English scientist, Thomas Young, made some important first steps. He found that some signs in oval frames, called cartouches, were royal names, like Ptolemy.

The real breakthrough was made by a French scholar, Jean-François Champollion. He knew several ancient languages, including Coptic, the last form of the Egyptian language. In 1822, he showed that hieroglyphs were not only pictures. Many signs also represented sounds, like letters, and some represented ideas. Now scholars could read thousands of ancient texts, and the history of ancient Egypt was open to the world again.

text: By the fourth century AD, the knowledge of how to read Egyptian hieroglyphs had been lost. For more than a thousand years, travellers marvelled at the inscriptions on temples and obelisks without understanding a word. Many scholars assumed that each sign represented an idea or a symbolic image, and some invented mystical interpretations that had nothing to do with the real meaning.

The breakthrough came by chance. Its surface carried a decree of 196 BC issued by priests in honour of King Ptolemy V, and the same text was inscribed three times, in hieroglyphs, in Demotic (a cursive form of Egyptian), and in ancient Greek. Because scholars could read Greek, they realised that the stone might provide the key to the other two scripts.

After the defeat of the French, the stone passed into British hands under the terms of the surrender in 1801 and has been in the British Museum since 1802. However, he still believed that most hieroglyphs were symbolic.

He compared the name 'Ptolemy' with the name 'Cleopatra' from another inscription and gradually worked out the sound values. In 1822, he announced that hieroglyphic writing combined signs for sounds with signs for ideas. This opened thousands of texts to historians, and the Rosetta Stone has since become a symbol of any key that solves a seemingly impossible puzzle. It remains one of the most visited objects in the museum and the subject of an ongoing dispute, as Egypt has requested its return.

text: In the seventeenth century, the Dutch Republic was one of the richest and most commercial societies in Europe. Wealth from overseas trade created a prosperous merchant class, and the tulip, introduced from the Ottoman Empire in the late sixteenth century, became a fashionable status symbol. Bulbs that produced flowers with unusual flame-like stripes were especially prized. We now know that these patterns were caused by a virus, which also weakened the plants and made such bulbs scarce.

In the 1630s, trading in tulips spread from specialist growers to a wider public, including craftsmen and shopkeepers. Because bulbs can only be dug up in summer, much of the trade took place in winter taverns through contracts promising delivery in the future, a system that resembled modern futures markets. During the winter of 1636-37, prices of rare varieties rose sharply, and some individual bulbs were reported to sell for as much as the price of a luxurious house in Amsterdam.

In February 1637, the market collapsed when buyers failed to appear at an auction in Haarlem, and the confidence on which the contracts depended disappeared. For two centuries, the episode was described as an example of mass irrationality, most memorably by the Scottish writer Charles Mackay in 1841. In his account, thousands of Dutch families were ruined, and the country's economy was damaged.

More recent research, notably by the historian Anne Goldgar, who examined surviving archives, has challenged this picture. She found very few documented cases of bankruptcy that could be traced to the collapse, and the courts and local authorities seemingly adopted a practical approach, allowing many contracts to be cancelled for a small fee. The mania, in this view, involved a limited group of wealthy traders and had little effect on the wider economy. This does not mean that the episode was unimportant. It remains a vivid symbol of speculation, but the story we usually hear says as much about how later writers needed such a lesson as about what really happened in the 1630s.
versions.proof: She found very few documented cases of bankruptcy that could be traced to the collapse, and the courts and local authorities seemingly adopted a practical approach, allowing many contracts to be cancelled for a small fee.

text: On 16 July 1969, a Saturn V rocket, the most powerful machine built up to that time, lifted Neil Armstrong, Buzz Aldrin and Michael Collins from Florida into space. Their destination was the Moon, and their mission had been defined by President Kennedy eight years earlier: to land a man on the Moon and return him safely to Earth before the end of the decade. Four days later, Armstrong and Aldrin entered the lunar module Eagle and separated from the command module Columbia, leaving Collins alone to orbit the Moon.

The descent did not go according to plan. While Eagle was descending, its on-board computer, which was far less powerful than a modern phone, repeatedly displayed alarms because it was being given more tasks than it could handle. A young controller in Houston, who had been trained to deal with exactly this problem, judged that the alarms were not serious and advised the crew to continue. Then Armstrong noticed that the automatic guidance was taking Eagle toward a boulder-strewn crater. He took manual control and flew horizontally across the surface, looking for a smoother site, while the fuel gauge fell lower and lower. The astronauts then rejoined Collins and travelled home, splashing down in the Pacific on 24 July. They were kept in quarantine for three weeks as a precaution. The achievement rested on the work of some 400,000 people, and for many of them, it was proof that large technical problems could be solved by organised, determined effort.

text: The bicycle seems such a simple machine that it is surprising how long it took to reach its present form. The next stage came in the 1860s, when French makers added cranks and pedals to the front wheel. Historians still dispute who deserves credit for this idea. The result was faster, but the wooden and iron wheels transmitted every bump of the road to the rider, which explains the nickname 'boneshaker'. During the 1870s, makers enlarged the front wheel to increase speed, because a larger wheel travelled further with each turn of the pedals. The decisive advance was the 'safety bicycle' of 1885, produced by John Kemp Starley, with two wheels of equal size and a chain driving the rear wheel. It was safer, lower, and easier to ride. Three years later, John Boyd Dunlop's air-filled rubber tyre made the ride far more comfortable, and falling prices brought bicycles within reach of clerks and factory workers. The 1890s became a period of 'bicycle mania'.

The social effects were considerable. Bicycles gave ordinary people a cheap means of travelling beyond their own neighbourhoods, and they contributed to demands for better roads. Historians debate how far this was true, but it shows how much contemporaries felt that this machine had altered everyday life.

The 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics, which she shared with Pierre and Henri Becquerel, brought fame, but Pierre was killed in a street accident in 1906, and Marie took over his professorship, becoming the first woman to teach at the Sorbonne. During the First World War, she helped to equip vehicles with X-ray machines so that surgeons could locate bullets in wounded soldiers. text: By 1666, London was one of the largest cities in Europe, but it was also one of the most vulnerable to fire. Most buildings were made of timber, many of them with roofs covered in pitch, and they stood tightly packed along narrow lanes, with upper storeys that almost touched across the street. After a summer of exceptional heat, the city was so dry that it needed only a spark.

In the early hours of Sunday, 2 September, a fire broke out in the bakery of Thomas Farriner in Pudding Lane. Farriner claimed that he had put out his oven the night before, but a spark apparently set fire to a pile of fuel. A strong east wind carried the flames to the warehouses along the river, which were full of tar, oil and spirits, and the fire became so fierce that it could not be stopped by the usual methods. The Lord Mayor, Thomas Bloodworth, was reluctant to order the demolition of houses to create firebreaks, because he feared that the owners would demand compensation, and the delay proved disastrous.

The disaster is vividly described in the diary of Samuel Pepys, a naval official, who watched from a boat on the Thames and saw people throwing their belongings into the river. He also buried his wine and a famous cheese in his garden. By the time the army was ordered to blow up buildings with gunpowder, the fire had destroyed much of the old city. It was finally stopped on 5 September, after about 13,200 houses, 87 parish churches and St Paul's Cathedral had been lost. The official records mention only six deaths, but historians suspect that the true figure was much higher, because the poor were probably not counted.

The rebuilding of London was equally dramatic. New laws required buildings to be constructed of brick or stone, and streets were widened. Christopher Wren designed a new St Paul's Cathedral and more than fifty new churches, and a tall column, the Monument, was built to commemorate the fire. The first fire insurance companies were also established soon afterwards. Although the fire was a catastrophe for those who lost their homes, it removed the overcrowded medieval city and, in some ways, laid the foundations for a more modern London.

text: Before 1914, a ship travelling from New York to San Francisco had to sail around the southern tip of South America, a dangerous voyage of about four months. For centuries, people had dreamed of cutting a canal through the narrow strip of land in Panama, which would link the Atlantic and the Pacific and remove the need for the long journey.

In 1881, a French company led by Ferdinand de Lesseps began the work. De Lesseps had triumphed with the Suez Canal, but Panama was a very different environment. It had heavy rainfall, unstable soil that kept sliding into the excavation, and a climate in which yellow fever and malaria spread rapidly among the workers. At that time, nobody knew that mosquitoes carried these diseases, and more than twenty thousand people may have died. De Lesseps also insisted on a canal at sea level, which was unrealistic in the mountainous terrain. In 1889, the company collapsed, and the project was abandoned in a financial scandal that ruined thousands of small investors.

In 1904, the United States took over, and it began with a campaign for public health. Doctor William Gorgas ordered that swamps be drained, homes be screened and standing water be sprayed with oil, and yellow fever almost disappeared from the area within a few years. The chief engineer, John Stevens, also changed the plan: instead of a sea-level canal, he proposed a system of locks that lift ships to a large artificial lake, which they then cross before being lowered again. This reduced the amount of excavation and made the project achievable.

The canal opened on 15 August 1914, and it shortened the voyage between the two coasts of the United States by roughly thirteen thousand kilometres. Its construction, however, had a high human cost: thousands of workers, many of them from the Caribbean, died even during the American period, and they were paid less than white employees.

The history of the canal is also a political one. The United States had supported Panama's separation from Colombia in 1903 and obtained control of a zone on both sides of the canal, an arrangement that many Panamanians resented for decades. It was only in 1999, after long negotiations, that the canal was handed over to Panama, and it remains vital to world trade today. In that sense, the story of the canal illustrates how a great engineering achievement can be inseparable from the medical, economic and political conditions in which it is built.

text: In the year 79 AD, Pompeii was a lively Roman town of about eleven thousand people on the Bay of Naples. It had a theatre, bars, bakeries and public baths. Behind it stood Mount Vesuvius, but the people did not know that it was a volcano, because it had been quiet for centuries. Then, one day, it exploded.

We know about the eruption from two letters written by a young Roman, Pliny the Younger, to the historian Tacitus. Pliny watched from across the bay and described a huge cloud shaped like a tree, which rose high above the mountain. His uncle, Pliny the Elder, commanded a fleet nearby and sailed towards the coast to help people escape, but he died there.

For hours, small, light stones fell on Pompeii, and roofs broke under the weight. Many people escaped. But early the next morning, fast, burning clouds of gas and ash rushed down the mountain and killed everyone who was still in the town. Pompeii was buried under several metres of ash.

text: In the year 79 AD, Pompeii was a prosperous Roman town of about eleven thousand people on the Bay of Naples, with a theatre, a forum, bakeries, bars and public baths. Behind it stood Mount Vesuvius, which the inhabitants did not recognise as a volcano, since it had been quiet for centuries. Earthquakes had damaged the town some years earlier, which may have been a warning that few understood.

The best surviving account comes from two letters written by Pliny the Younger to the historian Tacitus. He watched from across the bay and described a column of smoke, shaped like a pine tree, rising tens of kilometres into the sky. His uncle, Pliny the Elder, who commanded the fleet at Misenum, set out with ships to rescue people on the coast, and he died there, probably from the poisonous gas.

For hours, pumice, a light and porous stone, rained on Pompeii, and some roofs collapsed under the weight. Many inhabitants escaped during this phase. Early the next morning, however, surges of burning gas and ash raced down the mountain and killed those who had stayed behind, and the town was buried under several metres of volcanic material. The neighbouring town of Herculaneum was destroyed in a similar way.

The date of the eruption has long been given as 24 August, which appears in the surviving copies of Pliny's letter. But copies of an ancient text are not always reliable, and several details, such as the autumn fruit and heavy clothing found in the ruins, have never fitted well with late summer. In 2018, archaeologists discovered a charcoal inscription on a wall in a house under restoration, which seems to give a date in the middle of October. Because charcoal would have been wiped away or washed off quickly, the writer probably wrote it only shortly before the disaster. The question is still discussed, and some scholars remain cautious. Whatever the true date, the site gives an unusually clear picture of daily life in the Roman world.

text: On the cold morning of 17 December 1903, on a beach near Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, two brothers from Ohio made history. Since the engines available at the time were too heavy, they built their own light engine with the help of a mechanic named Charlie Taylor.

The first flight, with Orville at the controls, lasted twelve seconds and covered about thirty-seven metres. It was not impressive to watch, but it was the first time that a machine with an engine had taken off by its own power, flown under control, and landed safely. text: On the cold morning of 17 December 1903, on a windswept beach near Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, two brothers from Ohio made history. Wilbur and Orville Wright ran a bicycle shop in Dayton, and they had no university degrees, yet for years they had been studying one of the great technical problems of their age: how to build a flying machine that a pilot could control.

Many inventors had already tried. Some built engines powerful enough to lift a machine into the air, but their aircraft were unstable and difficult to steer, and several of them crashed. The Wrights realised that the key problem was not power, but control. Watching how birds twist their wings to turn, they designed a system that allowed the pilot to twist the wings of the aircraft in a similar way, and combined it with a movable rudder and an elevator at the front. In 1901, they built a small wind tunnel and tested hundreds of wing shapes, which enabled them to correct errors in the published tables of other researchers. Because no existing engine was light enough, they asked their mechanic, Charlie Taylor, to build one.

The first flight of the Flyer, with Orville at the controls, lasted twelve seconds and covered only about thirty-seven metres, less than the length of a modern passenger aircraft. Nevertheless, it was the first time a powered machine had taken off under its own power, flown under the pilot's control, and landed safely at a point as high as the take-off. The brothers made four flights that morning, taking turns, and the longest, flown by Wilbur, lasted fifty-nine seconds and covered roughly 260 metres, before a gust of wind damaged the machine.

The world was slow to notice. A well-funded rival project had failed in public only nine days earlier, and many newspaper editors and officials found it difficult to believe that two bicycle makers had succeeded. The brothers were cautious about showing their machine, partly because they wanted to protect their invention and secure a contract. It was only after public demonstrations in France and the United States in 1908 that the world accepted that powered flight had been achieved. The Wrights' real achievement was therefore not just one lucky flight, but a method: they identified the hardest problem, tested their ideas carefully, and solved it before building an aircraft around the solution.

text: Beriberi is a disease that weakens the muscles and nerves and can damage the heart. In the nineteenth century, it killed thousands of sailors, soldiers and prisoners in Asia, where many people ate mainly polished white rice. Doctors believed it was caused by a germ.

In the 1890s, a Dutch doctor named Christiaan Eijkman was working in a laboratory in Java, which was then a Dutch colony. He was looking for the germ of beriberi. One day, his chickens began to walk strangely and became weak, as if they had the disease. Some time later, the chickens recovered without any treatment.

Eijkman discovered what had changed. At first, the chickens had been fed white rice left over from the hospital kitchen. Then a new cook refused to give the army's rice to 'government' chickens and used cheaper brown rice instead. The brown rice still had its thin outer skin, but white rice had been polished and the skin removed. A survey of prisons in Java showed the same: prisons that gave white rice had more beriberi than prisons that gave brown rice.

Eijkman first thought that white rice contained a poison. But his colleague Gerrit Grijns understood that the skin of the rice contained something that the body needs. This substance was later called vitamin B1. In 1929, Eijkman shared the Nobel Prize with the British scientist Frederick Hopkins.

text: Beriberi is a disease that attacks the nerves and muscles and, in severe cases, the heart. In the nineteenth century, it killed thousands of sailors, soldiers and prisoners in Asia, where polished white rice had become the main food of many people. Most doctors, influenced by the recent success of Pasteur and Koch, were convinced that the cause must be a germ, and they spent years searching for it.

Christiaan Eijkman, a Dutch physician, was sent to the Dutch East Indies, today's Indonesia, in 1886 to look for the microbe. Some years later, working in a laboratory in Batavia, he noticed that his experimental chickens had begun to walk unsteadily and to lose strength, in a way that resembled beriberi in humans. He tried to infect healthy chickens with the sick ones, without success. Then, in 1897, the disease suddenly disappeared.

Eijkman investigated and found an explanation that was simple but surprising. Until then, the chickens had been fed polished rice left over from the military hospital's kitchen. A new cook, however, objected to giving army rice to what he considered government chickens, and used cheaper unpolished rice, with its brown outer skin. The chickens recovered. Eijkman tried both kinds of rice on his birds and confirmed that polished rice caused the disease, while unpolished rice protected against it.

A survey of prisons in Java gave the same result: those that served polished rice had many more cases of beriberi. At first, Eijkman believed that the white grain contained a poison and the skin an antidote, but his colleague Gerrit Grijns correctly suggested that the skin supplied something that the body needed. The missing substance, later called thiamine or vitamin B1, was isolated in the 1920s. In 1929, Eijkman shared the Nobel Prize with Frederick Hopkins.
versions.proof: Eijkman tried both kinds of rice on his birds and confirmed that polished rice caused the disease, while unpolished rice protected against it.

text: In the early nineteenth century, an operation was a terrible experience. There was no medicine to stop the pain. Patients were given alcohol, or they were held down by strong men, and surgeons worked as fast as they could. A good surgeon could remove a leg in less than a minute.

text: Before the middle of the nineteenth century, surgery was a terrifying experience. The answer was found, in a public and dramatic way, in Boston. On 16 October 1846, a dentist named William Morton gave a patient, Gilbert Abbott, a gas called ether to breathe through a glass device. When the operation was over, the patient reported that he had felt no pain. Warren is said to have turned to the audience and announced that this was no humbug.

The news travelled quickly. A letter describing the operation reached London within weeks, and in December 1846, the surgeon Robert Liston used ether to remove a man's leg. Success was followed by an unpleasant quarrel. text: In 1918, near the end of the First World War, a new kind of influenza began to spread around the world. It came in three waves, and the worst was in the autumn of 1918. It is estimated that about one third of the world's population caught the disease and that at least fifty million people died, more than the number killed in the war itself. Unusually, many of the victims were healthy young adults.

The disease is known as the 'Spanish flu', but there is little evidence that it started in Spain. The name came from the way newspapers reported it. In countries at war, such as Britain, France, Germany and the United States, governments controlled the news and did not want people to read bad news that could lower morale. Spain, however, was neutral in the war, so its newspapers could write freely about the illness. When the King of Spain, Alfonso XIII, was also reported to be ill, people in other countries thought that the disease came from Spain.

Where the disease really started is still unclear. Some scientists think it began in the United States, others in France or China. What is certain is that soldiers moving between countries, and crowded hospitals and trains, helped it to spread.

In many cities, schools and theatres were closed, and people were told to wear masks and avoid crowds. There were no antibiotics, and doctors could only treat the symptoms. By 1920, the disease had faded. Today, scientists study the 1918 virus to prepare for future pandemics.

text: In 1918, as the First World War was drawing to a close, a new strain of influenza began to spread around the world in three waves, the deadliest of which came in the autumn. It is estimated that about one third of the world's population was infected and that at least fifty million people died, considerably more than the number killed in the fighting. Strikingly, the death rate was highest not among the very young and the very old, as is usual with influenza, but among healthy adults between twenty and forty.

Although the disease became known as the 'Spanish flu', there is little evidence that it began in Spain. The name arose from wartime censorship. In Britain, France, Germany and the United States, the authorities restricted the news to protect morale, and newspapers published little about the epidemic. Spain, as a neutral country, had no such restrictions, and its newspapers reported the illness freely, particularly after King Alfonso XIII fell ill in May 1918. To readers elsewhere, it seemed that the disease had originated there.

The real origin remains a matter of dispute. Some historians point to an army camp in Kansas, others to a military hospital camp in France, and still others to China, and no consensus has been reached. What is certain is that troop movements, crowded trains and overcrowded hospitals allowed the virus to travel far and fast.

The responses of cities varied, and the differences were later studied carefully. In Philadelphia, officials allowed a huge parade to take place in late September, and within days, hospitals were overwhelmed. St. Louis, by contrast, closed schools and banned public gatherings early, and its death rate was much lower. The epidemic faded in 1919 and 1920, probably as the survivors gained immunity.
