Curiously, the pandemic was for decades largely absent from popular memory, overshadowed by the war that had preceded it. Historians have suggested several reasons: it arrived without a clear beginning or end, it killed people individually in their homes, and it left no monuments. Interest returned only in the late twentieth century, when scientists succeeded in recovering and studying the virus from preserved tissue. In the years that followed, several countries, including Britain, established ministries of health, partly because the epidemic had shown the need for coordinated national responses. text: For more than a thousand years, doctors followed the ideas of Galen, a Greek physician who lived in Rome in the second century. According to Galen, the liver made new blood all the time, and the body used it up like fuel. The blood moved back and forth in the veins, and it passed through tiny holes inside the heart.

William Harvey, an English doctor, did not accept this. He studied the hearts of animals and of dying people, and he watched how the heart moved. In 1628, he published a short book, 'On the Motion of the Heart', in which he made a calculation. Each time the heart beats, it pushes out a little blood. If you multiply this by the number of beats in an hour, the total is much more than the weight of a man.

The liver could not possibly make so much blood, and the body could not possibly use it all. Harvey decided that the same blood must go round and round: from the heart through the arteries to the body, and back through the veins. He also showed that the veins have small valves, which let blood flow in only one direction, towards the heart.

Many doctors attacked his ideas, and Harvey said that he lost some patients. But slowly, the circulation of the blood became accepted. Harvey could not explain how blood went from the arteries to the veins. This was shown only after his death, when Marcello Malpighi saw the tiny vessels under a microscope.

text: For more than a thousand years, European medicine followed the ideas of Galen, a Greek physician who worked in Rome in the second century. According to Galen, the liver continually produced new blood from food, and the body consumed it as a kind of fuel; the blood moved back and forth in the veins, and it seeped through invisible pores in the wall of the heart. William Harvey, an English physician, did. He studied the hearts of animals and of dying human beings, and he observed carefully how the heart moved. In 1628, he published a short book, 'On the Motion of the Heart', in which he made a simple calculation. If each beat of the heart pushed out even a small quantity of blood, then the amount pumped in an hour would be several times the weight of a man. Such quantities could not possibly be produced from food and consumed by the body.

Harvey therefore concluded that the same blood must be moving in a circle: from the heart through the arteries to the body, and back through the veins. He supported his argument with demonstrations. By pressing on a vein and pushing the blood along it with a finger, he showed that it could pass in only one direction, because of tiny valves that prevent backward flow. He also tied a band around an arm and showed that the veins swelled on the side farthest from the heart.

The book was attacked by many colleagues, who ridiculed it, and Harvey said that his practice suffered. Nevertheless, his ideas were gradually accepted. One weakness remained: he could not show how blood passed from arteries to veins. The tiny vessels that connect them, the capillaries, were seen under a microscope only in 1661, four years after his death, by Marcello Malpighi.

text: Diabetes was once a death sentence. In a person with type 1 diabetes, the body cannot make insulin, a hormone that helps the body use sugar from food. Before the 1920s, children who developed the disease usually died within a year or two. The only treatment was a very strict diet with almost no food, which kept patients alive a little longer but left them thin and weak.

In 1921, a young Canadian surgeon named Frederick Banting had an idea. He believed that a substance made by the pancreas could control sugar in the blood. He went to the University of Toronto, where Professor John Macleod gave him a small laboratory and a young assistant, Charles Best, for the summer. They tested extracts from the pancreas on dogs that had diabetes, and the dogs' blood sugar fell.

In January 1922, they gave their extract to Leonard Thompson, a fourteen-year-old boy who was dying in a Toronto hospital. The first injection was not pure enough and made him ill. A chemist in the team, James Collip, then cleaned the extract, and a second injection brought the boy's blood sugar down quickly. He soon looked healthier and stronger.

News of the treatment spread fast. Within months, companies began making insulin in large amounts. In 1923, Banting and Macleod received the Nobel Prize, and Banting shared his money with Best, while Macleod shared his with Collip. The inventors sold the patent to the university for one dollar, because they wanted everybody to be able to use it.

text: Doctors tried to move blood from one person to another for hundreds of years. Sometimes a patient who had lost a lot of blood was saved. But often the patient became very ill and died, and nobody knew why. Because of these deaths, blood transfusions were thought to be too dangerous, and they were hardly used.

In 1900 and 1901, an Austrian doctor named Karl Landsteiner worked in Vienna. He took blood from himself and his colleagues, and he mixed the red cells of one person with the liquid part of another person's blood. In some mixtures, the red cells clumped together, but in others they did not. After studying the results, he saw a pattern: people's blood belongs to different groups.

Landsteiner described three groups, A, B and C, which later became O. A fourth group, AB, was found a little later by his colleagues. If a person receives blood from an incompatible group, the body attacks the new cells, and the clumps can block small blood vessels. If the groups match, the transfusion is safe.

The discovery made safe transfusions possible. In 1907, an American doctor gave the first transfusion in which the blood of the donor and the patient had been tested. During the First World War, blood was stored and given to wounded soldiers. In 1930, Landsteiner received the Nobel Prize.

text: The idea of replacing lost blood with blood from another person is old. In the seventeenth century, physicians in France and England tried to transfuse blood from animals to humans, with fatal results in some cases, and the practice was banned. The explanation came from a quiet laboratory in Vienna. He described three groups, which he called A, B and C; the last was later renamed O, and a fourth group, AB, was found shortly afterwards by his colleagues. When the groups match, the transfusion is safe. This also explains the old failures: the earliest transfusions had been, in effect, a gamble.

The discovery made safe blood transfusion possible, although practice changed slowly. In 1907, the American physician Reuben Ottenberg performed the first transfusion in which the blood of donor and recipient had been tested for compatibility. During the First World War, blood was stored and given to wounded soldiers on a large scale, and blood banks followed. Landsteiner received the Nobel Prize in 1930, and in 1940, he and a colleague identified the Rh factor, another important feature of human blood.

text: In 1906, a wealthy banker in New York rented a summer house on Long Island. Soon, six of the eleven people in the house became ill with typhoid fever, a serious disease that spreads through dirty food and water. The owner was worried that nobody would rent the house again, so he hired an engineer named George Soper to find the cause.

Soper discovered that the family had hired a new cook, Mary Mallon, an Irish immigrant, three weeks before the first case. He also learned that she had worked in several other houses where people had fallen ill. When he found her, she was in perfect health, and she refused to believe that she could pass on a disease. Tests showed that her body carried the typhoid bacteria without making her sick. Today, such a person is called a healthy carrier.

In 1907, the health authorities took Mary to a small hospital on North Brother Island, where she stayed for three years. She was released in 1910 after promising not to work as a cook. But she changed her name and went back to cooking, because it paid better than the other jobs open to her. In 1915, a typhoid outbreak at a women's hospital in New York was traced to her. Mary spent most of the rest of her life on the island and died in 1938. Officially, she is linked with at least fifty cases of typhoid and three deaths. Her story shows how difficult it can be to balance public health and personal freedom.

text: Smallpox was a terrible disease. In Europe in the early eighteenth century, it killed many people every year, and those who survived often had deep scars. Lady Mary Wortley Montagu knew this well. Her younger brother had died of smallpox, and in 1715, she caught it herself and her face was scarred.

In 1716, her husband became British ambassador to the Ottoman Empire, and the family moved to Istanbul. In a letter from Edirne in 1717, she described a custom she had seen. Old women made a small cut in the skin of a healthy person and put in a little matter from a smallpox sore. The healthy person usually became only mildly ill and was then protected for life. Lady Mary was brave. In 1718, she had her five-year-old son inoculated in Istanbul, with the help of the embassy surgeon. Back in England, during an epidemic in 1721, she had her young daughter inoculated in front of royal doctors. The experiment was a success, and soon the Princess of Wales had her own children inoculated.

Inoculation was risky, because a few patients died, but it was much safer than catching the disease. In 1796, Edward Jenner developed vaccination, which used cowpox and was safer still. Lady Mary is remembered as one of the people who introduced protection against smallpox to Western medicine.

text: In the early eighteenth century, smallpox was one of the most feared diseases in Europe. It killed a large proportion of those who caught it, and the survivors were often blind or marked for life with deep scars. Lady Mary Wortley Montagu knew its effects personally: her younger brother had died of it, and in 1715, she herself caught it and was left with a scarred face.

In 1716, her husband was appointed British ambassador to the Ottoman Empire, and the family travelled across Europe to Edirne and then to Istanbul, which English speakers at that time called Constantinople. In a letter written from Edirne in 1717, she described a custom that she had observed. Every autumn, old women went from house to house with a nutshell containing matter from smallpox sores. They made a small scratch in the skin of a healthy person and introduced a little of the matter. The person usually developed a mild illness for a few days and was afterwards protected for life.

Lady Mary was convinced of its value, and she acted on her conviction. In 1718, she had her five-year-old son inoculated in Istanbul, with the assistance of the embassy surgeon. After her return to England, during a smallpox epidemic in 1721, she had her young daughter inoculated in the presence of royal physicians. The procedure was then tested on prisoners and orphans, and when it proved successful, the Princess of Wales had her own children inoculated, which made the practice respectable.

Inoculation was not without risk, since a small number of patients died, and some physicians and clergymen opposed it. But it was far safer than catching the disease naturally. Later, in 1796, Edward Jenner introduced vaccination with cowpox, which was safer still.

It would be wrong to give Lady Mary all the credit. Reports of inoculation had reached the Royal Society before her letters, from physicians who had worked in the Ottoman lands, and the practice was known in other parts of the world. What distinguished her was her social position and her determination to demonstrate it publicly, using her own children. In a society that was suspicious of ideas from abroad, that example carried unusual weight. She also defended the practice in an anonymous article in a London newspaper, because she knew that she would be criticised for supporting an idea that came from the Ottoman world.

text: In the early twentieth century, many poor people in the southern United States suffered from a terrible disease called pellagra. The patients had a painful rash on the skin and diarrhoea, and some became confused or mad. Many died. Most doctors thought that it was an infectious disease and that it was spread from person to person.

The nurses and other workers never got pellagra, although they lived in the same buildings as the patients. text: The English word 'quarantine' comes from the Italian words 'quaranta giorni', which mean 'forty days'. The idea began in the Middle Ages, when the Black Death killed millions of people in Europe. Cities that traded by sea were in special danger, because ships arrived every day from many places.

The first step was taken in 1377 in Ragusa, a trading city on the Adriatic coast, which is today called Dubrovnik. The officials ordered that travellers from areas with plague must wait thirty days, on an island or outside the city, before they could enter. Later, Venice, another trading city, made the waiting time forty days. Forty was a number with a special meaning in the Bible and in medical tradition.

At that time, nobody knew that plague was caused by bacteria carried by fleas. People believed that it spread through bad air or by touching the sick. But waiting really works: if a traveller is infected, he usually becomes ill within a few days or weeks, so a long wait shows who is sick before they enter the city.

In 1423, Venice also built a hospital for plague patients on a small island. Today, quarantine means keeping people who may be infected away from others for as long as necessary. It has been used for cholera, yellow fever and many other diseases.

text: The English word 'quarantine' comes from the Italian 'quaranta giorni', meaning 'forty days', and it recalls one of the earliest attempts to control an epidemic by organised public action. The background was the Black Death, which reached Europe in the 1340s and killed a large part of the population. Since trading cities received ships from all over the Mediterranean, they were especially exposed.

The first recorded measure was taken in 1377 in Ragusa, today's Dubrovnik, a prosperous trading city on the Adriatic coast. The city council ordered that travellers arriving from regions affected by plague should wait for thirty days, on an island or outside the walls, before they were allowed to enter. Later, Venice adopted a similar system and extended the waiting time to forty days, a number that had a long tradition in religious and medical writing.

What makes these rules remarkable is that nobody understood the cause of plague at the time. The bacteria were not identified until the 1890s, and fleas on rats were recognised as carriers later still. People generally thought that disease was spread through foul air or through contact. Nevertheless, the system worked after a fashion: a traveller who was infected usually became ill within days, so a long wait exposed the disease before it could enter the city.

Italian cities developed the idea further. In 1423, Venice opened a lazaretto on a small island, a place where the sick were cared for and ships' goods were kept apart, and other ports soon copied the model. Quarantine has since been used against cholera, yellow fever and many other diseases. It remains a difficult measure, because it limits personal freedom and trade, and its success depends on the willingness of people to accept it.

text: In 1917, a company in Orange, New Jersey, began to produce watches whose numbers glowed in the dark. In 1928, the case was settled: each woman received a sum of money and a promise of medical care and a yearly payment, although they were already gravely ill.

The 'Radium Girls' had lasting effects. Their cases established that employees can sue employers for illnesses caused by work, and they influenced later safety standards for workers exposed to radiation.

text: Today, the stethoscope is the symbol of a doctor. But two hundred years ago, doctors had no such instrument. To listen to a patient's heart or lungs, they simply put an ear against the patient's chest. This was unpleasant, and sometimes it was not possible at all.

In 1816, a French doctor named René Laennec was working at a hospital in Paris. He had to examine a young woman with heart problems, but he felt that it would not be polite to put his ear on her chest. Then he remembered that sound travels well along solid things. He rolled a sheet of paper into a tube, put one end on the woman's chest and the other end to his ear. He was surprised: he could hear her heart much more clearly than before.

Laennec made wooden tubes and tested them on many patients. After a patient died, he compared the sounds he had heard with what he found in the body. text: In the late 1950s, a new sleeping pill called thalidomide was sold in many countries. It was thought to be very safe, and doctors also gave it to pregnant women to reduce morning sickness. Nobody had properly tested whether it could harm an unborn baby.

Soon, thousands of babies were born with serious birth defects, especially with very short arms or legs. In 1961, a German doctor, Widukind Lenz, and an Australian doctor, William McBride, linked the defects to the drug, and it was taken off the market in Europe. It is estimated that about ten thousand children were affected around the world, and many of them did not survive.

In the United States, however, thalidomide was never approved. The reason was a government doctor, Frances Kelsey, who worked for the Food and Drug Administration. She had just started the job, and the company that wanted to sell the drug pressed her many times to say yes. But Kelsey thought that the company's safety information was not enough, and she asked for more tests. She waited until the news from Europe proved her right.

In 1962, President Kennedy gave her an award. That year, the United States also passed new laws, which required drug companies to prove that a medicine is effective as well as safe before it is sold. Many other countries made their rules stricter, too.

text: In the late 1950s, thalidomide, a new sedative, was sold in dozens of countries under various names. It was advertised as remarkably safe, since even large doses did not seem to harm laboratory animals, and doctors soon began to recommend it to pregnant women as a remedy for morning sickness. Nobody had carefully tested what effect it might have on an unborn child, because it was widely assumed at the time that a drug taken by the mother could not cross the placenta in a harmful way.

The consequences were tragic. From 1959, doctors in West Germany, Britain, Australia and other countries noticed a sudden rise in babies born with severe malformations, particularly very short or missing arms and legs. In 1961, a German paediatrician, Widukind Lenz, and an Australian obstetrician, William McBride, independently linked the defects to thalidomide, and the drug was withdrawn from the market in Europe at the end of that year. About ten thousand children are thought to have been affected worldwide, and a large number did not survive.

The United States was largely spared, thanks to one official. Frances Kelsey, a doctor who had just joined the Food and Drug Administration, was assigned to review the application of an American company that wanted to sell the drug. The company pressed her repeatedly to approve it, and even complained about her to her superiors, but she believed that the evidence of safety was inadequate and asked for further data. By the time the news from Europe arrived, her refusal had protected thousands of American families.

In 1962, President Kennedy awarded Kelsey a medal for distinguished service. Congress also passed a major reform of drug law, which required manufacturers to prove that new drugs are effective as well as safe, and to report adverse reactions. Similar reforms followed in other countries.

text: In the autumn of 1895, Wilhelm Röntgen, a German professor of physics, was experimenting with a glass tube from which most of the air had been removed. When an electric current passed through the tube, it produced invisible rays. Röntgen wanted to be sure that no light could escape, so on the evening of 8 November, he covered the tube with black cardboard and darkened his laboratory.

To his surprise, a screen covered with a special chemical, which was lying some distance away, began to glow. Something was passing through the cardboard and the air. Röntgen did not know what it was, so he called it 'X', the symbol scientists use for the unknown. For several weeks, he worked alone and found that the rays could pass through paper, wood and thin metal, but that lead stopped them.

In December, he asked his wife, Anna Bertha, to hold her hand still on a photographic plate. The picture showed the bones of her hand and her wedding ring. He sent it to other scientists, and within days, newspapers all over the world were talking about it.

Doctors quickly saw the value of the new rays. Soon, X-rays were used to find broken bones and bullets inside patients. Röntgen did not want to make money from his discovery, and in 1901, he received the first Nobel Prize in Physics. Early users, however, did not know the dangers, and many of them suffered burns.
versions.proof: To his surprise, a screen covered with a special chemical, which was lying some distance away, began to glow.

text: Mary Anning was born in 1799 in Lyme Regis, a small town on the south coast of England. Her father, a carpenter, died when she was a child, and the family was poor. They earned a little money by selling curiosities, which they found on the beach, to tourists. The cliffs of that coast contain rocks from the Jurassic period, and storms often uncover fossils of animals that lived about two hundred million years ago.

In about 1811, her brother Joseph found the skull of a strange animal in the cliff. A year later, when Mary was about twelve, she found the rest of the skeleton and spent months removing it from the rock. It was a sea reptile about five metres long, with a long nose, big eyes and limbs like paddles. It was later called Ichthyosaurus. People were amazed, because nobody had ever seen such an animal.

During the next thirty years, Mary found many other important fossils. In 1823, she discovered the first complete skeleton of a plesiosaur, which had a small head and a very long neck. In 1828, she found the first pterosaur skeleton outside Germany. She also helped scientists to understand fossilised droppings and what ancient animals ate.

But Mary was a poor woman, and she was not allowed to join the scientific societies. Her discoveries were published under other people's names. Only after her death in 1847 did people begin to honour her work.

text: Mary Anning was born in 1799 in Lyme Regis, a small town on the south coast of England. The cliffs of that part of the coast contain rocks from the Jurassic period, and storms and landslides regularly expose fossils of animals that lived about two hundred million years ago.

In about 1811, her older brother Joseph found the skull of an unusual creature in the cliff. A year or so later, when Mary was about twelve, she found the rest of the skeleton and worked for months to remove it from the rock. It was a marine reptile about five metres long, with a long snout, huge eyes and paddle-like limbs; later it was named Ichthyosaurus. Nobody then knew anything about such animals, and the discovery caused a sensation among scholars, though it was the landowner and the collectors who were paid, not the girl who had done the work.

Over the next three decades, Anning went on to find many other remarkable fossils. In 1823, she discovered the first complete skeleton of a plesiosaur, a reptile with a small head and a very long neck, and some scientists at first suspected that it was a forgery. In 1828, she found the first pterosaur skeleton discovered outside Germany. She also noticed that the stony objects called bezoar stones, which were found in the abdomens of some skeletons, were in fact fossilised droppings, and her observation helped scientists to understand what the ancient animals ate.

Although she was well informed and corresponded with leading geologists, she was not allowed to join the Geological Society of London, since it admitted only men, and her discoveries were published under other people's names. She died of cancer in 1847, and only after her death was her contribution publicly honoured. In 2010, the Royal Society included her in a list of the ten British women who have most influenced the history of science.

text: Mary Anning was born in 1799 in Lyme Regis, a small town on the south coast of England. Her father, a carpenter, died when she was a child, leaving the family in debt, and they earned a little money by selling curiosities that they found on the beach to tourists. The cliffs of that part of the coast contain rocks from the Jurassic period, and storms and landslides regularly expose fossils of animals that lived about two hundred million years ago.

In about 1811, her older brother Joseph found the skull of an unusual creature in the cliff. A year or so later, when Mary was about twelve, she found the rest of the skeleton and worked for months to remove it from the rock. It was a marine reptile about five metres long, with a long snout, huge eyes and paddle-like limbs; later it was named Ichthyosaurus. Nobody then knew anything about such animals, and the discovery caused a sensation among scholars, though it was the landowner and the collectors who were paid, not the girl who had done the work.

Over the next three decades, Anning went on to find many other remarkable fossils. In 1823, she discovered the first complete skeleton of a plesiosaur, a reptile with a small head and a very long neck, and some scientists at first suspected that it was a forgery. In 1828, she found the first pterosaur skeleton discovered outside Germany. She also noticed that the stony objects called bezoar stones, which were found in the abdomens of some skeletons, were in fact fossilised droppings, and her observation helped scientists to understand what the ancient animals ate.

Although she was well informed and corresponded with leading geologists, she was not allowed to join the Geological Society of London, since it admitted only men, and her discoveries were published under other people's names. She died of cancer in 1847, and only after her death was her contribution publicly honoured. In 2010, the Royal Society included her in a list of the ten British women who have most influenced the history of science.

Anning's fossils did more than fill museum shelves. At the time, many educated people believed that species do not change and that none had ever disappeared, and the discovery of whole skeletons of animals that no longer existed made extinction difficult to deny. Her finds therefore helped to prepare the way for the debates about the history of life that followed in the nineteenth century, including those provoked by Darwin's theory. That a working-class woman without formal education played such a part is one of the more striking facts in the history of science.

text: In 1964, two young scientists, Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson, worked at a laboratory in New Jersey. They had a very large horn-shaped antenna, which had been built to receive signals from satellites. They wanted to use it to study faint radio waves from our galaxy, so the instrument had to be as quiet as possible.

But they found a steady hiss that they could not remove. It came from every direction, day and night, in every season. They checked the electronics and looked for interference from New York City. Then they noticed that two pigeons had made a nest inside the antenna and that it was covered with a white material. They cleaned the antenna and removed the birds, but the hiss stayed.

At the same time, a group of scientists at Princeton University was preparing to look for exactly this kind of signal. According to the Big Bang theory, the early universe was very hot, and the radiation from that time should still be everywhere, although it should now be very cold. When Penzias spoke about his problem, a colleague saw the connection, and the two groups met.

The hiss was the cosmic microwave background, the oldest light in the universe. It is one of the strongest proofs of the Big Bang theory, and in 1978, Penzias and Wilson received the Nobel Prize in Physics.

text: In 1964, two young radio astronomers, Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson, were working at the Bell Telephone Laboratories in Holmdel, New Jersey. They had at their disposal a huge horn-shaped antenna, which had been built to receive signals from communication satellites. They wanted to use it to measure faint radio waves coming from our galaxy, so it was essential that the instrument should be as free of noise as possible.

To their frustration, they found a persistent background hiss that they could not remove. It was present day and night, in every direction, and in every season. They checked the electronics and pointed the antenna away from New York City, in case interference from the city was responsible. Then they noticed that a pair of pigeons had been nesting inside the horn, and that the antenna was covered with a white material, which Penzias politely described as 'white dielectric material'. They cleaned the antenna thoroughly and removed the birds, but the hiss remained.

At about the same time, a group of physicists at nearby Princeton University, led by Robert Dicke, was preparing to search for exactly such a signal. According to the Big Bang theory, the early universe had been extremely hot and dense, and the radiation left over from that time should still fill space, although it should by now be cooled to a few degrees above absolute zero. When Penzias mentioned his problem to a colleague, the connection was made, and the two groups met. Dicke is reported to have said to his team that they had been 'scooped'.

The hiss was the cosmic microwave background, the oldest light in the universe, released about 380,000 years after the Big Bang. It became one of the strongest pieces of evidence for the theory, and in 1978, Penzias and Wilson were awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics. Their discovery, like many others, shows how patient attention to an unexplained annoyance can lead to a scientific revolution.

text: On 22 December 1938, a fishing boat brought its catch into the port of East London, in South Africa. Among the fish was one that a young museum curator, Marjorie Courtenay-Latimer, had never seen. It was about one and a half metres long, steel blue, and covered with heavy scales, and it had strange fins that looked like legs. She did not know what it was, but she knew that it was special, and she took it to the museum.

She asked a scientist who studied fish, James Smith, to look at it. When he saw her drawing, he was amazed. The fish looked like a group of fish called coelacanths, which were known only from fossils. Coelacanths had lived more than four hundred million years ago, and the last fossils were about sixty-six million years old. Scientists thought that they had died out at the time of the dinosaurs.

Smith named the new fish Latimeria chalumnae, after the curator and the river near where it was caught. But one fish could not tell scientists very much, and Smith searched for another for many years. In 1952, a second one was found near the Comoro Islands, where local fishermen had caught these fish for a long time.

Scientists were excited, because the fins of the coelacanth have bones that look like the limbs of land animals. It is a famous example of a species that scientists believed was lost but that was still alive.

text: On 22 December 1938, a fishing boat brought its catch into the port of East London, in South Africa. Among the fish was one that the young museum curator, Marjorie Courtenay-Latimer, had never seen. It was about one and a half metres long, steel blue and covered with heavy scales, and it had thick, limb-like fins. She did not know what it was, but she recognised that it was extraordinary, and she took it to the museum, though it was a hot day and the taxi driver did not want to carry it.

Since she had no way of preserving a fish of this size, she asked an ichthyologist, James Smith, to examine it. These fish had appeared more than four hundred million years ago, and the last fossils were about sixty-six million years old, so it was assumed that they had become extinct at the time of the dinosaurs. A living coelacanth was therefore, as Smith said, as astonishing as finding a living dinosaur.

By the time the specimen reached Smith, the soft parts had decayed, and he was unable to confirm the identification until he had examined the skeleton. He named the species Latimeria chalumnae, after the curator and the river near where it had been caught. But a single fish could not answer many questions, and Smith spent years searching for another. It was not until 1952 that a second specimen was found, near the Comoro Islands in the Indian Ocean, where local fishermen had been catching the fish for years and sometimes used its rough scales as sandpaper.

Scientists were fascinated by the discovery, since the coelacanth has fins with a bone structure that resembles the limbs of land animals, and it was thought that it might tell them something about the origin of the first animals that walked on land. Later research showed that other groups of fish are even closer relatives of land animals, but the coelacanth remains a famous example of a species that was believed to be lost.

text: More than two thousand years ago, many Greek scholars knew that the Earth is round, but nobody knew how big it was. The first person to measure it carefully was Eratosthenes, a scholar who worked as the chief librarian of the great Library of Alexandria in Egypt. His method was very clever, because it needed only a stick, the Sun and a little geometry.

Eratosthenes heard that at noon on the longest day of the year, in the town of Syene, the Sun shone straight down into a deep well, so there were no shadows. But in Alexandria, a vertical stick did make a shadow at the same moment. He measured it and found that the Sun's rays made an angle of about seven degrees, which is about one fiftieth of a full circle.

He reasoned that the angle of the shadow was the same as the angle between the two cities at the centre of the Earth. The distance between Alexandria and Syene was about five thousand stadia, a Greek unit of length. We cannot be sure how accurate this was, because the stadion had different lengths in different places. According to one common estimate, his result was within a few percent of the true value of about forty thousand kilometres. Whatever the exact figure, he showed that people could measure the size of the planet by thinking, without travelling around it.

text: Most educated Greeks of the third century BC knew that the Earth is a sphere, but nobody knew how large it was. The first person to measure it with reasonable accuracy was Eratosthenes, a scholar from Cyrene who became the chief librarian of the great Library of Alexandria around 240 BC. His method was so elegant that it is still taught in schools, because it needs nothing more than a stick, the Sun and a little geometry.

Eratosthenes had heard that at noon on the summer solstice, in the southern town of Syene, today's Aswan, the Sun shone straight down into a deep well, so that no object cast a shadow. In Alexandria, however, a vertical stick did cast a shadow at the same moment. By measuring it, he found that the Sun's rays made an angle of about seven degrees, which is about one fiftieth of a full circle.

The reasoning that followed was simple. If the Sun is so distant that its rays are practically parallel, then the angle of the shadow must be the same as the angle at the centre of the Earth between the two cities. The distance between Alexandria and Syene was reported to be about five thousand stadia, and since this was one fiftieth of the Earth's circumference, the whole circumference must be about 250,000 stadia.

How accurate was the result? That depends on the length of the stadion, a unit that varied from place to place, and historians disagree about which one Eratosthenes used. According to one common estimate, his answer was within a few percent of the true value of about forty thousand kilometres, though other estimates give a larger error. Moreover, the two cities are not exactly on the same meridian, and the distance between them was probably measured roughly. Even so, his achievement remains remarkable, since it showed that the size of the planet could be found by reasoning rather than travel.

text: A hundred years ago, most astronomers thought that the whole universe was our own galaxy, the Milky Way. They believed that the faint, cloudy shapes they saw through telescopes were inside it. Edwin Hubble, an American astronomer, changed this idea. He worked with the biggest telescope in the world at that time, on Mount Wilson in California.

In 1923 and 1924, Hubble found a special kind of star in the Andromeda nebula. The brightness of this kind of star shows how far away it is. The result was surprising: Andromeda was much too far away to be part of the Milky Way. It was another galaxy. The universe was far bigger than anyone had thought.

Then Hubble studied the light from many galaxies. Another astronomer, Vesto Slipher, had found that the light of most galaxies was shifted towards red, which means that they are moving away. Hubble measured their distances too, and in 1929, he announced a remarkable result: the farther away a galaxy is, the faster it is moving away from us.

The simplest explanation was that space itself is expanding. If the galaxies are moving apart now, they must have been closer together in the past. This led scientists to the idea that the universe had a beginning, which is now called the Big Bang.

text: At the beginning of the 1920s, most astronomers believed that the entire universe consisted of our own galaxy, the Milky Way, and that the faint, cloudy patches seen through telescopes, called nebulae, were objects inside it. The simplest explanation was that space itself is expanding. If the galaxies are moving apart now, then they must have been closer together in the past, which implied that the universe had a beginning. Einstein's equations had allowed an expanding universe, but he had added a term to keep the universe static, because it seemed more natural to him. When he saw Hubble's results, he is reported to have called this term the greatest blunder of his life.

The history of the discovery is more complicated than the popular version. The Belgian priest and physicist Georges Lemaître had predicted an expanding universe on theoretical grounds in 1927, and he had derived a relation of the same kind two years before Hubble's paper. Today, the law relating distance and speed is often called the Hubble–Lemaître law.

text: Krakatoa was a volcanic island in the Sunda Strait, between Java and Sumatra in today's Indonesia. After a long quiet, it showed signs of activity in the spring of 1883, with clouds of ash and a sound of explosions. Authorities and local people paid it little attention, since volcanoes in the region were common. On 26 and 27 August, however, the activity grew into a series of enormous explosions, the last of which destroyed most of the island.

The final explosion, on the morning of 27 August, was probably the loudest sound in recorded history. It was heard on the island of Rodrigues, near Mauritius, almost five thousand kilometres away, where people thought that it was the firing of distant guns. The sudden change of pressure was recorded by barometers around the world, and the pressure wave circled the globe several times. The collapse of the volcano also generated huge sea waves, which devastated the coasts of Java and Sumatra and killed more than thirty-six thousand people.

The effects were not limited to the region. The eruption threw enormous quantities of ash and gas into the upper atmosphere, and winds carried them around the world. text: Krakatoa was a volcanic island in the Sunda Strait, between Java and Sumatra in today's Indonesia. text: 'Why is the sky blue?' is a question that children often ask, and it is not easy to answer. Some people think that the sky is blue because it reflects the sea. But the sky is blue also over deserts and mountains, far from any sea, so this cannot be the reason.

The real answer begins with sunlight. Sunlight looks white, but it is a mixture of all the colours of the rainbow, and each colour has a different wavelength. When sunlight enters the air, it hits the gas molecules in the atmosphere and is scattered in all directions. The British scientist Lord Rayleigh showed in the 1870s that short wavelengths, such as blue, are scattered much more strongly than long wavelengths, such as red.

So when we look at the sky away from the Sun, we mainly see blue light that has been scattered towards us. You may ask why the sky is not violet, because violet has an even shorter wavelength. The reasons are that the Sun gives out less violet light, the atmosphere takes in some of it, and our eyes are less sensitive to violet.

The same idea explains red sunsets. When the Sun is low, its light travels through a much longer layer of air, and most of the blue light is scattered away before it reaches our eyes. The light that remains is red and orange.

What remains is rich in red and orange, which is why the sky near the horizon glows with those colours.

text: Look at a map of the world, and you may notice that the east coast of South America and the west coast of Africa seem to fit together like pieces of a puzzle. text: 'Let them eat cake.' This is probably the most famous sentence that is connected with Marie Antoinette, the queen of France before the Revolution. According to the story, someone told her that the poor people of Paris had no bread, and she answered that they should eat cake. For two hundred years, people have repeated this story as an example of the ignorance of rich people.

But there is no evidence that she ever said it. The sentence first appears in the 'Confessions' of the writer Jean-Jacques Rousseau. He wrote about it around 1765, when Marie Antoinette was only a child of about ten, living in Austria. Rousseau says that 'a great princess' made the remark, but he does not give her name. He probably invented the story, or he repeated one that was already old.

Marie Antoinette's name was connected with the sentence only in the nineteenth century, long after her death. Also, the French word was 'brioche', a rich kind of bread, and the remark was probably meant as a silly joke about the price of bread.

The queen really was unpopular. She was born in another country, and she spent a lot of money while the state was almost bankrupt. She was executed in 1793. But the story about the cake is a good example of a false quotation which people continue to believe because it agrees with what they already think.

text: 'Let them eat cake.' The sentence is probably the most famous thing that Marie Antoinette, the queen of France before the Revolution, is supposed to have said. According to the story, when she was told that the poor of Paris had no bread, she answered, with great indifference, that they should eat cake instead. The remark has been repeated for more than two centuries as a symbol of the ignorance of the rich, and it is often used to explain why the people of France came to hate their queen.

However, there is no evidence that she ever said it. The sentence first appears in the 'Confessions' of the philosopher Jean-Jacques Rousseau, who wrote the relevant passage around 1765, at a time when Marie Antoinette was a child of about ten and still living in Austria. Rousseau reports that a 'great princess' had answered in this way when she was told that the peasants had no bread, but he does not give her name. In any case, he almost certainly invented the story, or repeated one that had been circulating for years.

Her name was attached to the phrase only much later, in the nineteenth century, when writers looking for a symbol of royal arrogance found the queen a convenient one. By that time, she had been dead for decades. In fact, the phrase also contains a mistake. The French word used by Rousseau was 'brioche', which was a rich bread made with butter and eggs, and the remark seems to have been intended as a clumsy joke about the high price of bread, not as a statement of cruelty.

Marie Antoinette was certainly unpopular. She was a foreign-born queen who spent large sums of money on clothes and entertainment, at a time when the state was nearly bankrupt, and her enemies spread many rumours about her. She was executed in 1793. Her actual record is, however, more complicated than the legend suggests, and some historians point out that she gave to charity and was no more extravagant than many other members of the court. The story of the cake is a good example of how a false quotation can survive because it fits what people already believe.

text: In 1951, a psychologist named Solomon Asch did a simple experiment. He told students that it was a test of eyesight. Each student looked at a card with one line and another card with three lines of different lengths. The student had to say which of the three lines was the same length as the first. The correct answer was always very easy to see.

But there was a trick. The student sat with seven to nine other people, and they were all actors. They knew the plan, but the student did not. In the first rounds, everyone gave the correct answer. Later, the actors all gave the same wrong answer, and the real student had to choose: to follow his own eyes or to follow the group.

The results were surprising. About a third of the students' answers followed the wrong group. About three quarters of the students gave at least one wrong answer. Only about a quarter never followed the group. Some students said that they had doubted their eyes, and others said that they did not want to look foolish.

Asch tried another version. This time, one actor gave the correct answer, and then most students said the correct answer too. The experiment shows that a group can have a strong influence on people, but that one person who disagrees can make a big difference.

text: In 1951, the psychologist Solomon Asch, who was working at Swarthmore College in the United States, designed a simple experiment on conformity, which means changing one's opinion or behaviour in order to match that of a group. Students were told that they were taking part in a test of eyesight. In each round, they were shown a card with a single line, and a second card with three lines of different lengths, and they had to say which of the three was the same length as the first. The correct answer was always obvious.

The real participant sat in a group of seven to nine people, who, without his knowledge, were actors working for Asch. The participant answered near the end. In the first rounds, everyone gave the correct answer. But in some later rounds, the actors, one after another, all gave the same wrong answer. The participant then had to choose between what he saw with his own eyes and what the whole group said.

The results surprised many people. About a third of all the answers given by the participants in these critical rounds followed the group's mistake, and about three quarters of the participants gave at least one wrong answer. Only about a quarter never followed the group at all. In interviews afterwards, some participants said that they had really doubted their own eyes, while others said that they had known that the answer was wrong but had not wanted to look foolish.

Asch also varied the conditions. When just one of the actors gave the correct answer, the participants were much more likely to say what they saw, and the amount of conformity fell sharply. This suggested that the group's influence depends on its unanimity. The study has often been repeated, and its results have been used to explain how people can be pressed into silence or agreement. At the same time, later researchers pointed out that most answers were independent, and that the participants were more resistant to pressure than the best-known description of the study might suggest.

text: In October 1347, a group of trading ships from the Black Sea arrived at the port of Messina, in Sicily. Many of the sailors were already dead or dying, and the survivors had dark swellings on their bodies. The people of the port tried to send the ships away, but it was too late. In a few years, the disease, later called the Black Death, spread across the whole of Europe.

No one knows exactly how many people died, because the records are not complete, but most historians think that between a third and a half of the people in Europe died between 1347 and 1351. Whole villages were abandoned, and in many towns, there were not enough healthy people to bury the dead. At that time, nobody understood the cause. Some people blamed the planets, and others blamed God.

The suffering was terrible, but the plague also changed the economy. Many workers had died, so the workers who survived were very important, and landowners had to compete for them. In England, wages roughly doubled in a few years, and many peasants left their lords to look for better conditions.

The king and Parliament made laws to keep wages at the old level, but these laws were difficult to enforce. Historians still debate the long-term effects, but many believe that the plague weakened the old system in which peasants were bound to the land.

It is not possible to say exactly how many died, because the records are incomplete, but most historians estimate that between a third and a half of the population of Europe was lost between 1347 and 1351. Whole villages were abandoned, and in many towns there were not enough healthy people to bury the dead. Nobody at the time understood this, and the explanations offered ranged from the position of the planets to the anger of God.

text: In October 1962, the world came closer to nuclear war than at any other time during the Cold War. The Soviet crew did not understand this. He argued with the others and persuaded them to bring the submarine to the surface and wait for instructions from Moscow.

The submarine surfaced, the Americans did not know how close they had come to a nuclear exchange, and the crisis ended peacefully a day later, when the two governments reached an agreement. The details of the incident became known only decades later, and the accounts of the men differ on some points, so historians remain cautious about it. Even so, many people believe that Arkhipov's decision, which was made in a hot, dark submarine without any orders, may have prevented a catastrophe. His story is often used to show how the fate of the world can depend on the judgement of one person.

text: From 1892 to 1954, more than twelve million immigrants passed through Ellis Island, in New York Harbor, on their way to a new life in the United States. They came after a long journey on crowded ships, and at Ellis Island, they had a medical check and answered questions from an inspector.

But historians say that this almost never happened. The inspectors at Ellis Island did not write down the names. The names had been written earlier, at the port where the immigrants started their journey, by clerks of the shipping companies. At Ellis Island, the inspector asked about thirty questions and compared the answers with the list. He had no reason to invent a new name.

text: Between 1892 and 1954, more than twelve million immigrants passed through Ellis Island, in New York Harbor, on their way to a new life in the United States. Their experience, which began with a long voyage in the crowded lower decks of a ship, ended with a medical check and a series of questions from an inspector, and it left a deep mark on the memory of millions of American families. One of the most common stories in these families is that an official at Ellis Island, unable to pronounce or spell a foreign name, wrote down a shorter or simpler version, so that the grandfather who arrived as 'Kowalczyk' became 'Cole' in a moment.

Historians who have studied the records say that this almost never happened. The inspectors at Ellis Island did not write down the names of the immigrants. The names were recorded earlier, at the port of departure, by clerks of the shipping companies, who prepared a list, or 'manifest', of all the passengers for each ship. These clerks were usually familiar with the languages of the region and had the passengers' documents in front of them, so errors were not common.

At Ellis Island, an inspector, who often spoke several languages, or was assisted by an interpreter, asked each person about thirty questions and compared the answers with the manifest. If there was a difference, the inspector corrected it, but the aim was to identify the passenger, not to change the name. Since the officials had the written list in front of them, they would have had no reason to invent a name on the spot.

If so many families believe the story, the explanation is probably that names were indeed changed, but by the immigrants themselves, in the years after arrival. Many wanted to find work, avoid prejudice or fit in with their neighbours, and they adopted names that were easier for Americans to pronounce, or translated them. Later generations, who had forgotten the reasons, may have found it easier to blame an official than to admit that their ancestors had made a deliberate choice. The myth, in other words, tells us less about Ellis Island than about the pressure on newcomers to become 'American'.

text: In the winter of 1901–02, French archaeologists excavating at Susa, in what is now south-western Iran, found three pieces of a large black stone, which together formed a pillar about two and a quarter metres tall. The surface was covered with a text in cuneiform, the wedge-shaped writing of ancient Mesopotamia, and at the top was a carving of a king standing in front of a seated god. The pillar had been made for Hammurabi, the king of Babylon, who ruled in the eighteenth century BC. It had probably been taken to Susa as a trophy by a later conqueror.

The text on the pillar contains nearly three hundred laws, which cover subjects as different as trade, marriage, property, wages and the behaviour of doctors and builders. One of the best known provisions says that if a builder constructs a house badly and it collapses and kills the owner, the builder shall be put to death. Another sets the payment for a surgeon's successful operation and a penalty if the operation fails. The laws were carved in public view so that, in theory, any literate person could know the rules which they would be judged by.

The code is often remembered for the principle of 'an eye for an eye', but this is only partly correct. In Hammurabi's laws, the penalty depended on the social class of both the offender and the victim. If a nobleman destroyed the eye of another nobleman, his own eye would be destroyed, but if he destroyed the eye of a commoner, he had only to pay a fine in silver. The code thus preserved a society which was divided into ranks, rather than an equality of all before the law.

Hammurabi's code was not the first collection of laws, since earlier ones, such as that of Ur-Nammu, are known. It is nevertheless one of the best preserved and the most complete, and it provides valuable evidence of daily life in ancient Babylon. It also expresses the idea, which is still important, that the king was responsible for justice and that written laws should protect the weak against the strong. The pillar is now displayed in the Louvre Museum in Paris.

text: In the winter of 1901–02, French archaeologists excavating at Susa, in what is now south-western Iran, found three pieces of a large black stone, which together formed a pillar about two and a quarter metres tall. The surface was covered with a text in cuneiform, the wedge-shaped writing of ancient Mesopotamia, and at the top was a carving of a king standing in front of a seated god. The pillar had been made for Hammurabi, the king of Babylon, who ruled in the eighteenth century BC. It had probably been taken to Susa as a trophy by a later conqueror.

The text on the pillar contains nearly three hundred laws, which cover subjects as different as trade, marriage, property, wages and the behaviour of doctors and builders. One of the best known provisions says that if a builder constructs a house badly and it collapses and kills the owner, the builder shall be put to death. Another sets the payment for a surgeon's successful operation and a penalty if the operation fails. The laws were carved in public view so that, in theory, any literate person could know the rules which they would be judged by.

The code is often remembered for the principle of 'an eye for an eye', but this is only partly correct. In Hammurabi's laws, the penalty depended on the social class of both the offender and the victim. If a nobleman destroyed the eye of another nobleman, his own eye would be destroyed, but if he destroyed the eye of a commoner, he had only to pay a fine in silver. The code thus preserved a society which was divided into ranks, rather than an equality of all before the law.

Hammurabi's code was not the first collection of laws, since earlier ones, such as that of Ur-Nammu, are known. It is nevertheless one of the best preserved and the most complete, and it provides valuable evidence of daily life in ancient Babylon. It also expresses the idea, which is still important, that the king was responsible for justice and that written laws should protect the weak against the strong. The pillar is now displayed in the Louvre Museum in Paris.

It is not clear how far the code reflected the practice of the courts. Judges in Babylon seem to have decided most cases on the basis of local custom and the evidence presented, and the surviving legal records rarely refer directly to Hammurabi's laws. Some scholars therefore think that the code was less a law book in the modern sense than a public statement, designed to show that the king was a just ruler. Whatever its original function, the text remained so respected that scribes copied it for more than a thousand years, which is a measure of its prestige.
versions.proof: The code is often remembered for the principle of 'an eye for an eye', but this is only partly correct.

text: In the 1920s, a large factory near Chicago, called the Hawthorne Works, made electrical equipment. The managers wanted to know if better working conditions would make their workers more productive. They began with a simple question: would more light help? A group of workers was tested with different levels of light.

The results were strange. When the lighting was brighter, the workers produced more. But when the researchers made the room darker, the workers also produced more. Their output went up even when it was so dark that they could hardly see. Later, the researchers changed the length of the breaks and the working hours, and again the workers usually produced more.

The explanation was that the workers were not reacting to light or breaks. They were reacting to the attention. Someone was watching them, and someone cared about their work, so they worked harder. This idea became known as the 'Hawthorne effect'.

Later, other researchers looked at the old data again, and they found that the story was not so simple. Other things may have changed the results, such as the dismissal of two workers or a new system of payment. Even so, scientists still think that people may behave differently when they know that someone is watching them.

text: In the 1920s and 1930s, researchers carried out a series of studies at the Hawthorne Works, a large factory near Chicago which belonged to the Western Electric Company. The managers wanted to find out how working conditions affected productivity, and they began with a simple question: would better lighting make the workers produce more? A group of employees, who assembled electrical equipment, was therefore tested under different levels of light.

The result was surprising. When the lighting was increased, output went up, as expected. But when the researchers lowered the light, output went up again, and it continued to rise even when the lighting was so dim that the workers could hardly see. The researchers later made other changes, such as changing the length of rest breaks and working hours, and again productivity generally improved, whatever they did.

The explanation, which became very influential, was that the workers were reacting not to the changes themselves but to the fact that they were being observed and that someone seemed to care about them. Being treated as important, the argument ran, made them work harder. This became known as the 'Hawthorne effect', and for decades it was cited in textbooks to show that social and psychological factors can matter as much as physical conditions in the workplace.

More recent research has made the story more complicated. When historians re-examined the original data, which was rediscovered in the 1980s, they found that the productivity figures did not clearly show the pattern described in the textbooks, and that other factors, such as the dismissal of two uncooperative workers and the introduction of payment based on group output, could have affected the results. Nevertheless, the idea that people may change their behaviour when they know that they are being watched is still taken seriously, and researchers have to design their studies carefully to avoid it.
versions.proof: The result was surprising.

text: Long ago, people who wanted to buy something often had to exchange goods or weigh pieces of metal. This was slow, and it was easy to cheat. Then, in the kingdom of Lydia, in the west of what is now Turkey, an important change took place. Around 600 BC, the Lydians began to make small pieces of metal with a stamp on them, usually the head of a lion. The stamp showed the weight and value of the piece. These were among the first coins in history.

The first Lydian coins were made of electrum, a natural mixture of gold and silver found in the sand of a river called the Pactolus. The mixture was not always the same, so the value could still change. But the merchants of Lydia, who lived on the road between Asia and the Aegean Sea, quickly saw the advantages of small coins. They were easy to carry, count and exchange.

A big improvement came in the time of King Croesus, in the middle of the sixth century BC. His officials learned to separate gold from silver, and the kingdom began to make coins of pure gold and pure silver. Trade became easier and more reliable. Croesus became so famous for his money that people still say 'as rich as Croesus'.
The idea of coins spread to the Greek cities and then to other countries. Historians are careful about the exact dates, but they agree that the Lydian coins changed trade for ever.

text: Until about twenty-six centuries ago, people who wanted to buy something usually had to exchange goods or weigh out pieces of metal, which was slow and left room for cheating. Then, in the kingdom of Lydia, in the west of what is now Turkey, a simple but important change took place. Some time around 600 BC, the Lydians began to produce small pieces of metal that were stamped with a mark, usually the head of a lion, to guarantee their weight and value. These were among the first coins in history.

The first Lydian coins were made of electrum, a natural mixture of gold and silver that was found in the sand of the river Pactolus. The proportion of the two metals, however, was not always the same, so the value of a coin could still vary. The stamp showed that the ruler vouched for the coin, but it did not remove all the doubt. The merchants of Lydia, who lived in a rich trading country on the road between Asia and the Aegean, were quick to see the advantages of small, standard pieces, since they were easy to carry, count and exchange.

A major improvement came during the reign of King Croesus, in the middle of the sixth century BC. His officials learned to separate gold from silver, and the kingdom began to produce coins of pure gold and pure silver, with a fixed weight. The system made trade simpler and more reliable, and it also allowed the state to pay its soldiers and officials in a form which they could use anywhere. Croesus himself became so famous for his wealth that the expression 'as rich as Croesus' is still used today.

The idea of coinage spread rapidly to the Greek cities of the coast and then to the rest of the Mediterranean and Asia, and, in the following centuries, it was adopted in India and China, in different forms. Historians remain cautious about the exact dates and about the question of who produced the very first coin, since the evidence is limited to a small number of finds, such as those from the temple of Artemis at Ephesus. What is clear is that the Lydians' invention made it possible to measure and exchange value in a way that had not been possible before.
versions.proof: A major improvement came during the reign of King Croesus, in the middle of the sixth century BC.

This turned the value of money into a matter of confidence rather than of weight alone, and it linked the economy to the authority of the state. text: In June 1215, King John of England met a group of angry barons at Runnymede, a meadow near London. The king was not popular. He had lost most of the English lands in France, and he asked for heavy taxes to pay for the wars. He also punished his enemies without a proper trial. The barons took the city of London, and the king had to talk to them.

The king put his seal on a long document, which was later called Magna Carta, or the Great Charter. It had sixty-three clauses. Most of them were about the barons' practical problems, such as money and justice. But some clauses were about important general ideas. One said that no free man could be put in prison except by the lawful judgement of his equals or by the law of the land.

As a peace treaty, Magna Carta failed. The king had agreed under pressure, and after a few weeks, he asked the Pope to cancel it. The Pope did, and the war started again. But after John died in 1216, the advisers of his young son reissued the charter, and later kings confirmed it many times.
Today, most of the clauses are no longer important, and only a few are still law. But the main idea, that even the ruler must obey the law, was used in many later struggles for freedom.

text: In June 1215, at Runnymede, a meadow beside the River Thames near London, King John of England met a group of rebellious barons and agreed to put his seal on a long document. The king was unpopular. He had lost most of the English lands in France, he had demanded heavy taxes to pay for the failed wars, and he had often punished his opponents without a proper trial. The barons had risen against him, taken the city of London and forced him to negotiate.

The document, which later came to be called Magna Carta, or the Great Charter, contained sixty-three clauses. Most of them dealt with practical grievances of the barons, such as the amount of money that the king could demand when a nobleman died, or the way in which justice was administered. A few, however, expressed more general principles. One famous clause stated that no free man could be imprisoned or deprived of his rights except by the lawful judgement of his equals or by the law of the land. Another said that the king would not sell, deny or delay justice.

As a peace treaty, Magna Carta was a failure. John had agreed to it only under pressure, and within a few weeks, he asked Pope Innocent III to declare it invalid, which the Pope did in August. The war between the king and the barons, which the charter had been intended to prevent, started again. When John died in 1216, however, the advisers of his young son, Henry III, reissued the charter in a modified form to win the support of the barons, and later kings confirmed it many times.

Over the centuries, the importance of Magna Carta grew far beyond its original meaning. Most of its clauses became obsolete, and only a few remain in English law today, but its basic principle, that even the ruler is subject to the law, was cited in many later struggles, including those which led to the English Civil War and the American Revolution. It is therefore remembered less for what it actually achieved in 1215 than for what later generations made of it.
versions.proof: As a peace treaty, Magna Carta was a failure.

One famous clause stated that no free man could be imprisoned or deprived of his rights except by the lawful judgement of his equals or by the law of the land. It is worth noticing how little the barons themselves intended. They were not trying to establish the rights of all English people, since the 'free men' of the charter were a minority, and most peasants were not included. They wanted to protect their own position against a king who had broken the customary rules. The wider meaning of the document was created later, when lawyers and politicians in different centuries found in its words a general defence of liberty. A text can acquire a significance that its authors never imagined, and Magna Carta is perhaps the clearest example.

text: On the evening of 1 December 1955, in Montgomery, Alabama, a forty-two-year-old seamstress named Rosa Parks boarded a city bus after work. In those years, the law of the southern states required black and white people to be separated in public places, and on buses, the front seats were reserved for white passengers, while black passengers had to sit at the back. When the bus filled up, the driver ordered Parks and three other black passengers to give up their seats to a white man. The others moved. Parks refused.

She was arrested and fined, but the story did not end there. A few months earlier, a teenager named Claudette Colvin had been arrested for the same reason, but the local leaders judged that Parks, who was respected and of good reputation, would be the best person to represent a legal challenge.

Within days, black residents of the city organised a boycott of the buses. They walked, shared cars and organised a system of taxis, and many of them travelled long distances to work every day. A new organisation, the Montgomery Improvement Association, was founded to lead the protest, and its president was a young minister named Martin Luther King Jr., who became a national figure as a result. The boycott lasted 381 days, causing the bus company severe financial losses.

In 1956, the Supreme Court confirmed an earlier ruling that segregation on city buses was unconstitutional, and the boycott ended in December of that year. The campaign did not by itself end racial segregation in the United States, which continued in other forms for many years, but it showed that peaceful and well-organised collective action could achieve concrete results, and it inspired the wider civil rights movement of the following decade.

text: In the summer of 1858, London was a city of about three million people, and almost all of their waste flowed into the River Thames, which also supplied much of the city's drinking water. For years, the situation had been getting worse, since the introduction of flush toilets had sent even more sewage into the river. In June of that year, a long period of hot weather arrived, and the smell from the river became unbearable. Newspapers called the episode 'the Great Stink'.

The smell was so strong that it reached the Houses of Parliament, which stood on the bank of the Thames. Members tried to work with curtains soaked in chemicals hung over the windows, and some committees left the building altogether. According to some accounts, there was even a proposal to move Parliament to another place. The politicians, who had often delayed spending money on sewers, found that the problem could not be ignored when it affected them personally.

The scientific theory of the time held that diseases such as cholera were spread by bad air, or 'miasma'. Although John Snow had argued in 1854 that cholera was carried by water, few people were convinced, and Parliament acted mainly because it feared that the stench itself would cause epidemics. Within about three weeks, it passed a law that gave the city's engineers the money and the powers that they needed. The engineer in charge, Joseph Bazalgette, designed a network of enormous sewers which collected the waste and carried it eastwards, away from the centre of the city, before releasing it into the river further downstream.

The project, which took about sixteen years, involved hundreds of kilometres of tunnels, built with hundreds of millions of bricks, and several large pumping stations. Its effects went beyond removing the smell. Since the sewage no longer polluted the water that people drank, cholera outbreaks in London became much less frequent. The reform, therefore, was inspired by a mistaken theory but produced a result that confirmed the new one. Much of Bazalgette's system is still in use today.

text: In April 1815, the volcano Tambora, on the island of Sumbawa in what is now Indonesia, erupted with a force that was greater than any other eruption in recorded history. The explosion was heard more than two thousand kilometres away, and the eruption and the famine which followed it killed tens of thousands of people in the region. At the time, however, few people in Europe or North America made any connection between this distant event and what happened to them next.

The following year, 1816, became known as 'the year without a summer'. In Europe and eastern North America, the spring was cold, and in many places, frosts and even snow appeared in June and July. Heavy rains ruined crops in Britain, France and Switzerland, and the price of grain rose sharply. In some regions, there were food riots, and many people left their homes to look for work or charity. Scientists now believe that the volcano had thrown enormous quantities of ash and sulphur into the upper atmosphere, where they reflected sunlight and cooled the planet.

The cold weather also had cultural consequences. In the summer of 1816, a group of young writers, including Lord Byron, Percy Shelley and Mary Shelley, were staying near Lake Geneva, but the endless rain kept them indoors. To entertain themselves, they agreed to write ghost stories, and Mary Shelley began the story that became 'Frankenstein'. Byron also wrote a poem called 'Darkness', in which the sun goes out.

Some historians have suggested that the shortage of food also affected technology. Since many horses had to be killed or could not be fed, the German inventor Karl Drais is said to have been inspired to build a machine which could be used without a horse. His running machine, which appeared in 1817, was an early ancestor of the bicycle, though the link with the volcano remains a hypothesis. What is certain is that the eruption of a single mountain affected harvests, art and the history of ideas on the other side of the world.

The episode is a useful reminder that climate and society are connected in ways that are easily forgotten. At the time, nobody could explain the cold, and many people turned to religion or superstition. It was only much later that scientists were able to reconstruct the links between the eruption and the weather, using records from ice cores and tree rings. Today, historians sometimes use 1816 as a case study of how a society reacts when a sudden natural shock reduces the food supply, and of how little the distant causes of such a shock may be understood by those who suffer from it.

text: By December 1914, the First World War was only a few months old, but it had already become a war of trenches. text: At the beginning of the twentieth century, the last great prize of exploration was the South Pole, and in 1911, two expeditions set out to reach it. One was British and was led by Captain Robert Falcon Scott, a naval officer; the other was Norwegian and was led by Roald Amundsen, an experienced polar explorer. Amundsen had originally planned to go to the North Pole, but when he heard that two Americans had claimed to have reached it, he secretly changed his destination, and told even his own crew only when the ship had already left Europe.

The two teams used very different methods. Amundsen's men travelled on skis and used dogs to pull their sledges, an approach that he had learned from the Inuit people of the Arctic. The dogs were strong and well suited to the cold, and some of them were killed on the way to feed the other dogs and the men. Scott, on the other hand, relied on motor sledges, which broke down early, on ponies, which suffered terribly in the cold, and finally on the men themselves, who had to pull their heavy sledges on foot.

Amundsen and four companions reached the South Pole on 14 December 1911, and they planted the Norwegian flag and left a tent with a letter for Scott. They returned safely, having covered the distance more quickly and with greater ease than anybody had expected. Scott and four men arrived at the Pole on 17 January 1912, after weeks of exhausting effort, and they found the tent and the flag of their rivals. Scott wrote in his diary, 'Great God! This is an awful place,' and the party began the long journey back.

None of them survived the return. Weakened by hunger, frostbite and extremely bad weather, they died one after another, and the last three, including Scott, perished in their tent in late March, only about eighteen kilometres from a depot of food. Their bodies were found eight months later, together with their diaries, and Scott became a national hero in Britain. Historians, however, have often argued that the success of Amundsen owed less to luck than to careful planning, while the tragedy of Scott's party was due, at least partly, to poorer organisation and decisions that depended too much on hope.
