text: In 1957, two American engineers, Alfred Fielding and Marc Chavannes, who lived in New Jersey, had an idea for a new product. They wanted to make a kind of wallpaper with a textured surface, which would be attractive, easy to clean and different from anything else on the market. To make it, they sealed two plastic shower curtains together in a machine, which trapped air between the layers. The result was a sheet of plastic covered with small bubbles of air.

As wallpaper, the product was not a success. Customers did not like the look of the bubbles, and nobody bought it. The two men, however, did not give up. They believed that the material was useful, and they tried to find another use for it. They suggested it as insulation for greenhouses, since the air in the bubbles would keep the heat in, but this idea did not work either, and the market remained very small.

In 1960, they founded a company, Sealed Air, and began to look for customers who needed to protect fragile objects. A turning point came when Fielding, who was a very good salesman, brought the material to the attention of IBM, which had just launched a new computer, the IBM 1401. Computers at that time were large, delicate and extremely expensive, and the company was looking for something that would protect them when they were shipped to customers. The bubbles absorbed shocks, were light and cheap, and could be applied easily.

text: In July 1518, in the city of Strasbourg, which at that time belonged to the Holy Roman Empire, a woman called Frau Troffea walked into a street and began to dance. Within a week, about thirty other people had joined her, and within a month, according to some estimates, the number had grown to around four hundred.

The dancers did not seem to enjoy it. According to the records, which include the city council's notes and the chronicles written at the time, they cried out for help, and their feet were often bleeding. The authorities, who did not know what to do, asked local physicians, and the doctors concluded that the cause was 'hot blood' and that the dancers needed to dance until the heat had left them. The council therefore did something that seems strange to us: it opened guildhalls, built a wooden stage, and paid musicians to play, in the hope of helping the dancers to finish.

The remedy made things worse, and the number of dancers increased. Later, the authorities changed their approach. They decided that the cause was supernatural, banned public music and dancing, and sent the afflicted people, in carts, to a mountain shrine dedicated to Saint Vitus, where they were given red shoes and prayed over. Some chroniclers wrote that several of the dancers died from heart attacks, strokes or exhaustion, although it is difficult to know how many, and the evidence is weak.

Historians have offered several explanations. One theory is that the dancers had eaten bread contaminated with ergot, a fungus that can cause hallucinations and convulsions, but most scholars reject it, since ergot poisoning would not explain how people could dance continuously for days. Another, more widely accepted, suggestion is that the dancing plague was a case of mass psychogenic illness, brought on by extreme stress. The region had suffered famine and disease in the years before 1518, and the population believed strongly in saints who could punish sinners with a compulsion to dance. In the end, however, the real cause remains a mystery.

text: The Eiffel Tower, now the symbol of Paris, was never meant to stay for ever. It was built for the Universal Exhibition of 1889, which celebrated the hundredth anniversary of the French Revolution. The engineer, Gustave Eiffel, had permission to keep it for only twenty years. Many people were against the project. In 1887, a group of artists and writers published a letter in a Paris newspaper. When the permit was near its end, Eiffel had a plan. He asked scientists to do experiments on the tower, especially with wireless telegraphy, and a radio antenna was fixed to the top. text: The Eiffel Tower, which is now the symbol of Paris and one of the most visited monuments in the world, was never intended to stay. It was built for the Universal Exhibition of 1889, which was held to mark the hundredth anniversary of the French Revolution, and its designer, the engineer Gustave Eiffel, had received permission to keep it standing for only twenty years. After that, it was to be taken down, and the land would be returned to the city.

The project was controversial from the start. In 1887, a group of well-known artists and writers published a letter of protest in a Paris newspaper, in which they described the tower as a 'useless and monstrous' structure that would dishonour the city's architecture. Whether or not the story is true, it shows how strongly some people felt.

Nevertheless, the construction was remarkably fast. About three hundred workers assembled more than eighteen thousand iron parts in two years, two months and five days, and the tower, which was three hundred metres high, became the tallest man-made structure in the world, a position that it held until 1930. During the exhibition, nearly two million people climbed it or went up in its lifts, and it was a great success, even though many Parisians still disliked its appearance.

When the permit approached its end, Eiffel had already thought of a way of saving his work. He encouraged scientists to use the tower for experiments in meteorology, aerodynamics and, above all, the new technology of wireless telegraphy. A radio antenna was fixed to the top, and the army realised that a tall tower, which could transmit signals over long distances, was extremely useful. In 1909, the permit was therefore extended, and the tower was kept. Its usefulness as a transmitter, rather than its beauty, saved it. Today, it still carries antennas for radio and television, although it is its appearance that people come to see.

text: Today, billions of emails are sent every day, and almost every address has the symbol '@'. But in 1971, when the first email was sent over a network, hardly anyone used this symbol. The man who sent that message was an American engineer named Ray Tomlinson. He worked at a company in Cambridge, Massachusetts, which helped to build ARPANET, the early network that became the ancestor of the internet.

Electronic messages already existed, but they could only be left for other users of the same computer. Tomlinson was working on a program for this, and he also worked on a program that sent files between computers on the network. He saw that he could join the two, so that a message could go to a person on a different machine. But there was a problem: the address had to show both the name of the user and the name of the computer.

He needed a symbol to separate the two parts, which could not be a part of anybody's name. He looked at his keyboard and chose the '@', which means 'at' in English. In those days, it was almost never used for anything else. The system was logical and simple, and soon other programmers started to use it.

Tomlinson said that the first message was probably something like 'QWERTY', the first letters of the keyboard, and he did not save it. He sent it between two machines that stood next to each other. He did not think that he had done anything important, but within a few years, email was the most popular use of the network.

text: Today, billions of messages are sent by email every day, and almost every address contains the symbol '@'. Yet in 1971, when the first network email was sent, the symbol was seen on keyboards but was seldom used, and only a few people knew how to type a message from one computer to another. The man who sent that message, an American engineer named Ray Tomlinson, was working at a company in Cambridge, Massachusetts, called Bolt, Beranek and Newman, which helped to build ARPANET, the early network that became the ancestor of the internet.

Electronic messages already existed at that time, but they could only be left for other users of the same computer, like notes in a mailbox. Tomlinson was working on a program which allowed users to do this, and he had also been working on a program which transferred files between computers on the network. He saw that the two programs could be combined, so that a message could be sent to a person who used a different machine. The problem was how to indicate in the address both the name of the user and the name of the computer on which that person's mailbox was.

He needed a symbol that would separate the two parts and that could not appear in anybody's name. Looking at his keyboard, he chose the '@', which, in English, means 'at', and which was almost never used for anything else in those days. The address of the recipient, for example, could be written as 'user at computer'. The arrangement was logical, simple and easy to remember, and, although Tomlinson did not think that he had done anything important, it was soon adopted by other programmers.

Tomlinson later said that the first message was probably something like 'QWERTYUIOP', the top row of letters on the keyboard, and that he did not keep a record of it. He sent it between two machines that were standing side by side in the same room, since he wanted to test the system before trying it over the network. When he told a colleague, he reportedly added, 'Don't tell anyone! This isn't what we're supposed to be working on.' Within a few years, email had become the most widely used application on the network. Tomlinson was inducted into the Internet Hall of Fame in 2012, and he died in 2016.

text: After the First World War, the Australian government gave farmland in Western Australia to thousands of former soldiers, who tried to make a living by growing wheat. The farmers were then hit by the Great Depression, and in 1932, they faced another problem. About twenty thousand emus, large flightless birds, which usually spend the winter inland, migrated towards the coast and began to enter the wheat fields, where they ate the crops and broke down the fences. The farmers, many of whom were veterans, asked the government for help.

The government sent the army. In November 1932, a small unit of soldiers, led by Major G. P. W. Meredith, was sent to the region with two Lewis machine guns and about ten thousand rounds of ammunition. It was intended as a kind of military exercise, and the newspapers, which were amused by the idea, soon called it the 'Emu War'. The soldiers, however, discovered that the emus were much harder to hit than they had expected. When they were attacked, the birds divided into small groups and ran in different directions at great speed, and, since they could survive several bullets, many escaped even when they were hit.

On one occasion, the soldiers waited near a dam, and when a flock of about a thousand emus approached, the gun jammed after only a few birds had been hit. In another attempt, they mounted a gun on a truck, but the vehicle was too slow, and the bumps in the road made it impossible to aim. Major Meredith later said, with some admiration, that if there were an army with the fighting qualities of these birds, it could face any army in the world.

After about a week, the operation was suspended, and the soldiers were withdrawn. A second attempt was made later in the same month, and according to the reports of the unit, several hundred birds were killed, although these figures were probably not exact. Whatever the numbers, the emus remained a problem, and the government finally had to adopt a different approach: a system of rewards for each bird killed by the farmers themselves, which was much more successful. The incident, which is sometimes described as a defeat of the army by birds, is better described as a lesson in the limits of military solutions to an agricultural problem.

text: In December 1914, the British explorer Sir Ernest Shackleton left South Georgia in the South Atlantic on a ship called the Endurance. His aim was to cross the whole continent of Antarctica on foot, from one coast to the other, an expedition that had never been tried. With him were twenty-seven men, and they expected to land on the coast of the Weddell Sea within a few weeks. But in January 1915, the ship became trapped in the pack ice, a day's sail from the land, and could not be freed.

For months, the men lived on the ship as it drifted slowly with the ice, hoping that spring would release it. Instead, the pressure of the ice gradually crushed the hull. In October 1915, Shackleton ordered everyone to leave the ship, and in November, the Endurance sank. The men were left on the ice with three lifeboats, some food and equipment, and no means of communicating with the outside world. Nobody knew where they were, and nobody was looking for them.

Shackleton's main aim then changed, from crossing Antarctica to bringing all of his men home alive. They camped on the drifting ice for five months, and when it began to break up in April 1916, they took to the boats and, after a terrible journey of a week, reached the uninhabited Elephant Island. It was the first time that they had stood on land in almost sixteen months, but the island was far from any shipping route, so waiting there would have meant certain death.

Shackleton therefore decided to take one of the lifeboats, the James Caird, and sail with five companions to South Georgia, more than a thousand kilometres away, across some of the most dangerous seas in the world. They reached the island after sixteen days, but landed on the wrong side, and had to cross unmapped mountains on foot to reach a whaling station. After several failed attempts, Shackleton returned to Elephant Island in August 1916 and rescued the twenty-two men who had been left there. Remarkably, not one man of the whole expedition had died. The story is often told as a model of leadership, because Shackleton had kept up the morale of his men in a seemingly hopeless situation.

The bricks now held firmly together, but could still be easily separated, and it was possible to combine them in an almost unlimited number of ways. The bricks that are made today are so precisely produced that they can still be fitted together with those made in 1958. text: On Monday, 21 August 1911, the Louvre, one of the most famous museums in the world, was closed for cleaning. When the truth became clear, the Louvre was closed for a week, and the police interviewed hundreds of people. The theft turned the painting into a sensation. Newspapers around the world reported it on their front pages, and crowds queued to look at the empty space on the wall. Until then, the Mona Lisa had been admired by connoisseurs but was far from being the most famous painting in the world. Peruggia kept it in a wooden box in his small room in Paris for more than two years, and it was only in December 1913 that he tried to sell it to an art dealer in Florence.

The dealer recognised it, informed the director of the Uffizi gallery, and Peruggia was arrested. He explained that he had wanted to return the painting to its homeland, since he believed that Napoleon had stolen it, which was not true, because Leonardo himself had brought it to France. He received a light sentence, and many Italians regarded him as a patriot. After being exhibited in Italy, the Mona Lisa was returned to the Louvre in 1914, and its fame has been enormous ever since. Ironically, the crime that was supposed to be a disaster for the museum made its most famous painting even more famous.

text: Monopoly is one of the best-selling board games in the world, and for many years, the story of its origin was well known. According to the official version, an unemployed heating engineer from Philadelphia named Charles Darrow invented the game in the 1930s during the Great Depression, sold it to the company Parker Brothers in 1935 and became the first millionaire in the history of game design. The story fitted the American idea that anyone could succeed through talent and hard work, and it was repeated in the rule book and in newspapers for decades.

In fact, the game had a much longer and more interesting history. Its real ancestor was a game called 'The Landlord's Game', which was patented in 1904 by a woman named Elizabeth Magie, known as Lizzie. Magie was an author, a stenographer and a political activist, who admired the economist Henry George, who argued that land should belong to everyone and that landowners should be taxed heavily on its value. She designed the game to show, in a simple and playable form, how the system of rent enriched landlords and impoverished tenants.

Her game had two sets of rules. In one, which she called the 'monopolist' version, players won by taking all of the money and eliminating the others. In the other, the 'prosperity' version, wealth was shared, and everyone won when the poorest player doubled his or her money. Magie hoped that people would see the difference and learn which system was fairer. Many players, however, preferred the first version, and this is the one that survived.

Over the following years, the game spread informally among college students and intellectuals, who changed the rules and the names of the squares, and different versions appeared in various cities. Darrow learned the game from friends in Philadelphia, and, after changing it a little, he sold it as his own. When Parker Brothers discovered that Magie's patent existed, they bought it from her in 1935 for five hundred dollars, without paying any royalties, so that no one could challenge their claim. For decades, Magie's role was almost completely forgotten, and it was only after research by historians in recent years that she began to receive credit. It is a considerable irony that a game that was meant to criticise monopoly was transformed into a celebration of it.

text: Today, we take millions of photographs every day, and the exposure of each one takes a tiny fraction of a second. The oldest photograph which has survived to our time, however, was made in a very different way. It was taken around 1826 or 1827 by a French inventor named Nicéphore Niépce, from a window on the upper floor of his house in the village of Saint-Loup-de-Varennes in Burgundy. The picture shows the roofs and walls of the farm buildings and a tree, as seen from the window, and it is now known as 'View from the Window at Le Gras'.

Niépce, who was a gentleman with a passion for experiments, had for years been trying to find a way of fixing the images that appear inside a camera obscura, a darkened box with a small hole or lens which projects the outside scene onto a surface. The problem was that the image disappeared as soon as the light stopped, and no substance was known that would record it permanently. Niépce's solution was to use a plate of pewter, a soft metal, coated with a thin layer of bitumen, a kind of natural asphalt.

Bitumen has the property of hardening when exposed to light. Where light was strongest, the bitumen became hard, and where it was dark, it remained soft. After the exposure, Niépce washed the plate with a mixture of oil of lavender and white petroleum, which dissolved the soft parts and left the hard ones, so that the image appeared in the form of light and dark areas. The exposure, however, was extremely long. It was traditionally believed that it lasted about eight hours, which is why the sun seems to light both sides of the buildings in the picture, but more recent research has suggested that it may have taken several days.

Niépce did not live to see the real success of photography. In 1829, he made an agreement with another Frenchman, Louis Daguerre, who continued to develop the process after Niépce's death in 1833 and, a few years later, produced a method that needed only minutes of exposure and gave much sharper images. The earlier picture of the window was nearly forgotten. It was rediscovered in 1952, and it is now kept at a university library in Texas, where it is protected from light in a special container.

At breakfast one morning in March 1930, she heard her grandfather, a former librarian at the Bodleian Library, reading in the newspaper about the discovery, and she suggested that the planet should be called Pluto, after the Roman god of the underworld, since it was so dark and cold. Her grandfather passed the idea to a professor of astronomy, who telegraphed it to America. The staff of the observatory liked the name, partly because its first two letters were the initials of Percival Lowell, and they voted for it.

For decades, Pluto was the ninth planet, but in the 1990s, astronomers began to find other objects of similar size in the same distant region of the solar system, called the Kuiper Belt. In 2005, a body called Eris was discovered, which seemed to be even larger than Pluto. This presented astronomers with a choice: either to accept that there were dozens of planets, or to define more precisely what a planet is.

In August 2006, the International Astronomical Union voted to adopt a definition. According to it, a planet must orbit the Sun, be large enough to have a round shape, and have cleared the neighbourhood around its orbit of other objects. Pluto satisfied the first two conditions but not the third, and so it was reclassified as a 'dwarf planet'. The decision caused great public controversy, and some astronomers still disagree with it. It did not, however, change the object itself, which was visited in 2015 by the spacecraft New Horizons, and revealed to be a complex and surprisingly active world with mountains of ice and a large heart-shaped plain.

The controversy shows that scientific categories are human tools, not natural facts. Nothing about Pluto changed in 2006, but the word which the astronomers used to describe it did, and many people felt a sense of loss, as if a familiar member of the solar system had been taken away. For scientists, however, the new definition was a sign of progress: a better knowledge of the outer solar system made the old category inadequate. It is a reminder that scientific language has to be revised when new discoveries make old definitions unsatisfactory.

text: The Great Pyramid of Giza, built for the Egyptian king Khufu around 2560 BC, was for nearly four thousand years the tallest building in the world. It originally stood about 146 metres high and consisted of more than two million blocks of stone. For centuries, it was believed that such a huge monument could only have been built by an enormous army of slaves, forced to work under the whip. This idea came largely from the Greek historian Herodotus, who visited Egypt some two thousand years after the pyramid was built and wrote that a hundred thousand men had worked on it for twenty years.

In the 1990s, however, archaeologists working near the pyramids, led by Mark Lehner and Zahi Hawass, made discoveries that suggested a different picture. They found the remains of a large settlement, which included bakeries, breweries, houses and storerooms, and, nearby, the cemeteries where the builders had been buried. The workers had been given proper tombs, which were placed close to the pyramids of their king, and a number of them contained bread, beer jars and tools for use in the afterlife. Such burials would have been unlikely for slaves.

The evidence shows that the workers were well fed. Excavations produced the bones of large numbers of cattle, sheep and goats, and it has been estimated that the workers received meat regularly. Some skeletons show broken bones that had healed carefully, which suggests that injured workers received medical care. The labourers were organised in teams, and the names that were painted on the walls of the chambers above the king's chamber, such as 'Friends of Khufu', indicate pride in their work.

Most scholars now believe that the permanent workforce consisted of a few thousand skilled craftsmen, who were assisted by larger groups of farmers who came for several months at a time, perhaps during the season when the Nile flooded their fields. For them, the work may have been a form of national service, and in return, they received food. This does not mean that the work was easy, or that nobody was forced to take part, but the picture of a pyramid built by slaves is now regarded as a myth.

text: In 1941, a Swiss engineer named George de Mestral went for a walk in the Alps with his dog. It took about ten years to make it work. At first, he used cotton, but it wore out quickly. Many people thought that his idea was silly, but he continued, and in 1955, he received a patent.

He called his invention 'Velcro', from the French words 'velours' (velvet) and 'crochet' (hook). It was used in space, in clothes, in shoes and in medical equipment. Today, it is a famous example of learning from nature.

text: In 1941, a Swiss engineer named George de Mestral went for a walk in the Alps with his dog. When they returned, he found that his trousers and the dog's coat were covered with small, round burrs, the seed cases of a plant called burdock, which stuck to everything that they touched. Like many people before him, de Mestral found this irritating, and it took him a long time to remove them. Unlike most people, however, he wondered how they worked.

Out of curiosity, he looked at a burr through a microscope. He saw that its surface was covered with hundreds of tiny hooks, which caught on the loops of the cloth or the fur. Nature had produced a simple and effective fastening, and de Mestral began to think about making something similar. He imagined a system of two strips, one with hooks and one with loops, which would hold together firmly but could be pulled apart when necessary.

Turning the idea into a product took about ten years. At first, he tried to use cotton, but it wore out quickly. After many experiments, he found that nylon, a new synthetic material, was much stronger if it was heated under infrared light, because the hooks then kept their shape. He also had to design a loom that could produce the tiny hooks and loops in large numbers. Many of the people to whom he showed the idea thought that it was silly, but he persisted, and in 1955, he obtained a patent.

De Mestral called his invention 'Velcro', a word made from the French words 'velours', meaning velvet, and 'crochet', meaning hook. At first, it was used only in specialised products, since many people considered it ugly. Its reputation changed when it was used in space, where astronauts needed to fasten tools and objects in conditions without gravity, and then in clothes, shoes and medical equipment. The story of Velcro is one of the best known examples of 'biomimicry', the practice of learning from nature in order to solve human problems.

text: Before the middle of the twentieth century, doctors paid little attention to the first minutes of a baby's life. They judged a newborn baby only by general impression. Virginia Apgar, an American doctor, noticed this problem in a New York hospital. In 1952 she proposed a simple scoring system. text: Until the middle of the twentieth century, the first minutes of a baby's life received surprisingly little systematic attention. Doctors and midwives judged a newborn by general impression, and a baby who seemed weak or lifeless was sometimes set aside, while attention was given to the mother. There was no common way of describing how well a newborn was doing, so it was hard to compare the results of different methods or to notice a baby who needed urgent help.

Virginia Apgar, an American doctor who had become one of the first women to specialise in anaesthesia, worked in the delivery rooms of a New York hospital and noticed this problem. In 1952 she proposed a simple scoring system. One minute after birth, an observer would give the baby a score from zero to two for each of five signs: heart rate, breathing effort, muscle tone, response to stimulation, and skin colour. The scores were added to give a total from zero to ten.

The system was quick, required no special equipment, and could be used by anyone present at the birth. A score of seven or more showed that the baby was in good condition, while a low score warned that help, such as clearing the airway or giving oxygen, was needed at once. The assessment was usually repeated after five minutes, which showed how the baby was responding to treatment. Later, the letters of her surname were used to remember the five signs, although the test was named after her from the start.

Apgar's score was adopted in hospitals around the world, and it helped to make the care of newborns a recognised medical concern. Studies showed that babies with low scores were more likely to need intensive care, and attention to resuscitation improved. Apgar herself later turned to research on birth defects, working for an organisation that raised money to fight them, and she continued to work until her death in 1974.

text: On 3 December 1967, in a hospital in Cape Town, South Africa, a surgeon named Christiaan Barnard did the first heart transplant in the world. His patient was Louis Washkansky, a grocer aged fifty-three. His heart was very weak after many heart attacks, and he was close to death.

The new heart came from Denise Darvall, a young woman who died in a road accident. Her father agreed to give her heart. The operation took several hours, and a large team worked with Barnard. When the new heart was connected, doctors used a small electric shock to make it start beating.

At first, the patient was much better and could even speak. But there was a serious danger: the body often attacks a new organ. To stop this, doctors gave him drugs that made his immune system weaker. These drugs also made it hard for him to fight infection, and he caught pneumonia. He died eighteen days after the operation.

Still, the operation was seen as a great step, and surgeons in many countries began to try heart transplants. Later, a new drug made transplants much safer, and today they are a normal treatment for some patients.

text: On 3 December 1967, in Groote Schuur Hospital in Cape Town, a South African surgeon named Christiaan Barnard performed the first transplant of a human heart. His patient was Louis Washkansky, a fifty-three-year-old grocer whose heart had been ruined by repeated heart attacks and who was close to death. The donor was Denise Darvall, a young woman who had been fatally injured in a road accident and whose father agreed to the use of her heart. Barnard, then forty-five years old, had trained in the United States and had practised the technique for years on animals, but nobody could be sure that it would work in a human being.

The operation lasted several hours and involved a large team. Barnard removed Washkansky's failing heart, connected the new one to the blood vessels, and then shocked it into beating. Reporters from around the world soon gathered outside the hospital, and within hours the story was in newspapers on every continent. The patient woke up able to speak, and at first he seemed to improve, which raised hopes that the operation might become a regular treatment.

The greatest danger, however, was rejection, since the body treats a foreign organ as an enemy. To prevent it, doctors gave Washkansky drugs that weakened his immune system. These drugs also reduced his ability to fight infection, and he developed pneumonia. He died eighteen days after the operation, although the transplanted heart was still working.

Barnard's achievement was nonetheless regarded as a breakthrough, and it encouraged surgeons in many countries to begin heart transplants. Many of the early patients died within weeks, and some doctors criticised the operations as premature. In the 1980s, however, a new drug, cyclosporine, controlled rejection far more effectively, and the survival rate rose to the point at which heart transplantation became a standard treatment for patients with severe heart failure.

text: In the 1840s, most people thought that women could not be doctors. Medical schools did not accept women, and many people believed that women were too delicate to study the human body. text: Ibn Sina, known in Europe as Avicenna, was born around 980 near Bukhara, in present-day Uzbekistan. He was a gifted child. According to his own story, he had learned the Qur'an and much of the knowledge of his time by the age of ten. He studied medicine as a teenager, and he found it easier than many other subjects.

While he was still young, he is said to have cured the ruler of Bukhara, and as a reward he could use the royal library. Later, his life was not peaceful. He moved from city to city, worked for different rulers as a doctor and adviser, and sometimes went to prison. Even so, he wrote a great deal. More than a hundred works are connected with his name.

His greatest medical book, the 'Canon of Medicine', was finished around 1025. It collected the knowledge of Greek, Persian and Indian doctors and put it in a clear order in five books. It described hundreds of drugs and many illnesses, and it gave rules for testing a new medicine.

In the twelfth century, the book was translated into Latin. For about six hundred years, medical students in Europe and in the Islamic world used it. Ibn Sina died in 1037, but he is still remembered as one of the most important people in the history of medicine.

text: Ibn Sina, known in Europe as Avicenna, was born around 980 near Bukhara, in present-day Uzbekistan. He was a gifted child who, according to his own account, had memorised the Qur'an and mastered much of the learning of his time by the age of ten. He studied medicine as a teenager and found it easier than other subjects, because, as he later said, it was not one of the difficult sciences. While still a youth he is said to have cured the ruler of Bukhara of an illness that other physicians could not treat, and he was rewarded with access to the royal library.

Ibn Sina's life was far from peaceful. After the fall of the dynasty that had supported him, he moved from city to city in Central Asia and Iran, serving rulers as a physician and an adviser, and sometimes suffering imprisonment. Despite these difficulties, he wrote with remarkable energy. Over a hundred works are attributed to him, covering philosophy, science and medicine, and he often composed them at night after long days at court.

His greatest medical work, the 'Canon of Medicine', was completed around 1025. It gathered the knowledge of Greek, Persian and Indian physicians and arranged it in a clear and logical order in five books, which dealt with general principles, single drugs, diseases of each part of the body, fevers and surgery, and compound medicines. The Canon described hundreds of drugs, discussed the symptoms of many illnesses, and proposed rules for testing a new medicine, such as trying it on a simple condition first.

In the twelfth century, the Canon was translated into Latin, and for roughly six centuries it remained a standard textbook in the medical schools of Europe, as well as in the Islamic world. Ibn Sina died in 1037 in Hamadan, in present-day Iran, but his reputation lived on. Today, he is remembered as one of the most influential figures in the history of medicine, and in Turkey, as in many other countries, his name is borne by hospitals and schools.

text: In the nineteenth century, tuberculosis killed many people in Europe. About one death in seven may have been caused by it. People called the disease 'consumption', because it slowly consumed its victims. Nobody knew its cause, so nobody knew how to stop it. Some people thought that it ran in families, and others blamed bad air.

Robert Koch, a German doctor, decided to look for a germ. This was difficult, because the germ was very small and almost invisible under a microscope. It also grew very slowly. Koch tried new dyes, and he found that a blue dye made the thin rods easy to see in the tissue of sick patients.

He grew the germ on a special solid material and put it into healthy animals, which then became ill. In the animals, he found the same rods again. On 24 March 1882, he told scientists in Berlin about his discovery.

Koch did not find a cure. However, people now knew that tuberculosis was an infectious disease caused by a germ. Sick people were separated from others, and campaigns for cleaner and less crowded homes began. In 1905 Koch received the Nobel Prize for his work, and his method of proving that a germ causes a disease is still taught today.

text: In the nineteenth century, tuberculosis was one of the deadliest diseases in Europe, and it is often estimated to have caused about one death in seven. It was called 'consumption', because it seemed to consume its victims slowly. Many people believed that it ran in families, and others blamed bad air or a weak character. Nobody knew for certain what caused it, and so nobody knew how to prevent it.

Robert Koch, a German doctor who had already shown that a bacterium caused anthrax, decided to look for a germ behind tuberculosis. The task was difficult. The organism was extremely small, it was almost invisible under a microscope unless it was stained, and it grew far more slowly than other bacteria, so that cultures were often ruined by faster-growing organisms before the tubercle germ appeared. Koch therefore tried new dyes, and he found that a blue stain made the thin rods stand out clearly in tissue taken from diseased patients.

He then grew the organism on a special solid medium made from blood serum, and he injected it into healthy animals, which developed the disease. When he examined them, he found the same rods in their tissue. On 24 March 1882, he announced his discovery to the Berlin Physiological Society. The audience, it is said, was so moved that nobody asked a question. His careful procedure was later summarised as 'Koch's postulates', a set of rules for proving that a particular microbe causes a particular disease.

Koch's discovery did not provide a cure, and a remedy that he announced in 1890, tuberculin, failed to treat the disease, although it later became useful as a test. Nevertheless, by showing that tuberculosis was an infectious disease caused by a specific germ, he changed public health: sick people were isolated, and campaigns against spitting and overcrowding began. For this work he was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1905.

text: In the middle of the nineteenth century, a surgical operation was often very dangerous. Even when the operation went well, many patients died a few days later because their wounds became infected. Doctors called this 'hospital disease'. Surgeons did not wash their hands, and they wore their everyday clothes in the operating room. Nobody knew yet that dirt could carry disease from one patient to another.

Joseph Lister, a young surgeon in Glasgow, was worried about these deaths. In the 1860s he read the work of Louis Pasteur, who had shown that very small living things cause fermentation and decay. Lister thought that the same small living things might enter a wound and cause infection.

So he decided to kill them. He used carbolic acid on the wounds, the bandages and the instruments, and later he even sprayed it into the air of the operating room. In 1865 he treated a boy with a badly broken leg in this way, and the wound healed without infection.

Some doctors were slow to accept his ideas, because the acid hurt the skin and they did not believe in invisible germs. But slowly, more surgeons used his method, and fewer patients died. Today, clean instruments and clean hands are a normal part of every operation.

He then showed that moving a magnet in and out of a coil produced the same effect.

This was electromagnetic induction, the principle behind the electric generator and the transformer. Faraday did not use advanced mathematics, but he thought in terms of invisible 'lines of force' that filled the space around magnets and currents. Later, the physicist James Clerk Maxwell turned these ideas into equations. Faraday also gave the Royal Institution's popular Christmas lectures for young people, a tradition that continues today. Many visitors were struck by his clear explanations and his simple demonstrations, such as the burning candle, which he used to explain basic chemistry to ordinary audiences.

text: In 1609, Galileo Galilei, a professor in Padua, heard that a Dutch spectacle-maker had made an instrument that made faraway things look closer. Within a few months, he built one himself, and he improved it until it made things look about twenty times bigger. Most people thought that the new instrument was useful for seeing ships or armies. Galileo had another idea: he pointed it at the sky.

What he saw was surprising. The Moon was not smooth and perfect; it had mountains and craters. The Milky Way, which looks like a pale cloud, was made of countless stars. Then, in January 1610, Galileo saw three small bright points near Jupiter. Night after night, he wrote down their positions. They moved from one side of the planet to the other, and a fourth one appeared a few days later.

Galileo decided that these were moons that moved around Jupiter. At that time, most people believed that everything in the sky moved around the Earth. Here was a group of objects that did not. In March 1610, Galileo published his discovery in a short book, and he became famous in Europe.

Later, his observations of Venus supported the idea that the planets move around the Sun. This brought him into conflict with the Church. In 1633, he was tried in Rome and kept at home for the rest of his life.

text: Johannes Kepler was born in 1571 in what is now Germany. He was a mathematician who believed that the universe had an order. In 1600, he went to Prague to work with Tycho Brahe, the best observer of the sky at that time. For many years, Brahe had written down the positions of the planets very carefully, but he did not like to share his records with a younger man.

When Brahe died suddenly in 1601, Kepler could use the records. He wanted to understand the orbit of Mars. For centuries, people had believed that the heavenly bodies moved in perfect circles. Kepler tried many circles. After years of hard calculation, he found a model that was almost right. But it was a little different from Brahe's observations, and Kepler could not ignore this.

He trusted Brahe's data, so he gave up the circle. He found that Mars moves in an ellipse, with the Sun at one special point. This became his first law. His second law says that a planet moves faster when it is near the Sun. Later, a third law connected the time of an orbit to the distance from the Sun.
These laws changed astronomy, and they helped Newton to explain gravity.

text: Johannes Kepler, born in 1571 in what is now Germany, was a mathematician with a deep belief that the universe was ordered according to a divine plan. Brahe had spent decades recording the positions of the planets with unmatched accuracy, but he was reluctant to share his data with a younger man.

When Brahe died suddenly in 1601, Kepler obtained access to the records, and he set out to explain the orbit of Mars, whose path had always troubled astronomers. For centuries, it had been taken for granted that heavenly bodies moved in perfect circles. Kepler tried circle after circle, and after years of laborious calculation he found a model that fitted to within a small margin of error. Yet it disagreed with Brahe's observations by an amount that Kepler could not ignore.

Trusting the quality of Brahe's data, he gave up the circle. After further attempts, he found that the orbit of Mars was an ellipse, with the Sun at one of its two foci. This became his first law. In 1609, he published the second law, which states that a planet sweeps out equal areas in equal times, so that it moves faster when it is closer to the Sun. A decade later, a third law linked the time of a planet's orbit to its distance from the Sun.

Kepler's laws overturned a belief that had lasted since antiquity. They also gave Isaac Newton the evidence he needed for his theory of gravity, which explained why the planets move as Kepler had described. Kepler's life was not easy: he lost several children, he had to defend his mother against a charge of witchcraft, and he was often short of money. Nevertheless, his persistence changed astronomy.

text: Antoine Lavoisier was born in Paris in 1743. He studied law, but his real interest was science, and he became one of the most important chemists of the eighteenth century. At that time, many chemists explained burning with a theory of 'phlogiston', an invisible substance that a burning material was believed to give off. Metals that became a powder when heated were thought to have lost this substance.

Lavoisier did not trust explanations that could not be measured, and he used the balance carefully. He heated metals such as tin in closed vessels and weighed everything before and after. The metal became heavier when it turned into powder, and the air in the vessel became lighter by the same amount. This could not be explained by the loss of a substance. Something from the air had joined the metal.

Lavoisier found that a part of the air, which he called oxygen, combines with burning substances. He also showed that water is made of hydrogen and oxygen. His most important principle was the conservation of mass: in a chemical reaction, matter is not created or destroyed.

text: Antoine Lavoisier, born in Paris in 1743, trained as a lawyer, but his true interest was in science, and he became one of the most important chemists of the eighteenth century. text: In the 1860s, Dmitri Mendeleev, a professor of chemistry in St Petersburg, faced a practical problem: he was writing a textbook and needed a logical way to present the chemical elements. Lithium, sodium and potassium, for example, were all soft metals that reacted violently with water.

According to a popular story, he spent days arranging and rearranging the cards, as if playing a game of patience. In 1869, he found that when the elements were placed in order of increasing atomic weight, similar properties recurred at regular intervals. He arranged them in rows and columns, which became the periodic table.

What set Mendeleev apart was his courage. Where the pattern demanded it, he left gaps in the table, and he insisted that these gaps belonged to elements that had not yet been discovered. text: In the 1860s, Dmitri Mendeleev, a professor of chemistry in St Petersburg, faced a practical problem: he was writing a textbook and needed a logical way to present the chemical elements. According to a popular story, he spent days arranging and rearranging the cards, as if playing a game of patience. text: On 20 September 1519, five ships left the Spanish port of Sanlúcar de Barrameda under the command of Ferdinand Magellan, a Portuguese navigator in the service of the Spanish crown. The remaining men, short of crew, burned one ship and continued with two.

Under the Basque navigator Juan Sebastián Elcano, only one ship, the Victoria, completed the voyage, and it reached Spain in September 1522. Only about eighteen men were on board. They had become the first to sail around the world. The expedition's chronicler, Antonio Pigafetta, who survived the journey, noticed something curious: although he had kept an accurate daily record, their calendar was a day behind the one on land. They had lost a day by travelling westwards.

text: The ancient Olympic Games, held in Olympia in Greece, were celebrated for more than a thousand years, until they were ended in the late fourth century AD, when the Roman Empire had become Christian. For about fifteen hundred years after that, they were almost forgotten. The man who brought them back was a French aristocrat, Baron Pierre de Coubertin, who was born in 1863 and who took an unusual interest in education and sport.

Coubertin admired the English public schools, where sport was considered part of a young person's character training, and he believed that France's defeat in the Franco-Prussian War of 1870–71 was partly due to the weakness of its young men. He also hoped that international sporting contests might promote understanding between nations. In 1894, he organised a congress at the Sorbonne in Paris, where delegates from several countries voted to revive the Olympic Games and to hold the first ones in Athens in 1896.

Preparations were difficult. Greece was a poor country, and the government was reluctant to pay for the Games. Wealthy private donors helped, and the great marble stadium of ancient Athens, the Panathenaic Stadium, was rebuilt for the occasion. The Games opened on 6 April 1896, in front of tens of thousands of spectators. About 240 male athletes from around fourteen countries took part, and the events included athletics, swimming, cycling, fencing, gymnastics and shooting. Women were not allowed to compete.

The most memorable event was the marathon, a new race inspired by the story of a messenger who is said to have run from the battlefield of Marathon to Athens to announce a victory. The Greek runner Spyridon Louis won, to the delight of the crowd, and became a national hero. Coubertin later served as president of the International Olympic Committee, and the Games grew into one of the largest events in the world. Women first competed in 1900.

It was said to have been made by pasting sheets of paper together into a long roll, so that it could be rolled out across the floor of the House. At the time, this was a remarkable number: about a quarter of the adult European women in the colony signed it.

In September 1893, the Electoral Bill, which gave women the right to vote, was passed and signed by the governor. text: In the nineteenth century, women in almost every country were excluded from voting. The campaign for change was long and difficult. In New Zealand, it was led by Kate Sheppard, who was born in Liverpool, moved to Christchurch with her family in 1868, and became a leading figure in the Women's Christian Temperance Union. The union's members wanted, among other aims, to reduce the harm caused by alcohol, and they believed that women needed the vote to achieve this.

Over several years, Sheppard and her colleagues organised petitions that were sent to Parliament. In 1891 and 1892, the petitions gathered thousands of signatures. In 1893, the largest petition, which carried nearly 32,000 names, was presented to Parliament. It was said to have been made by pasting sheets of paper together into a long roll, so that it could be rolled out across the floor of the House. At the time, this was a remarkable number: about a quarter of the adult European women in the colony signed it.

The campaign faced strong opposition from some politicians, and from some brewers and hoteliers, who feared that women voters would support restrictions on alcohol. Some politicians, including the Premier, Richard Seddon, initially opposed the reform, but support among members of Parliament was growing. In September 1893, the Electoral Bill, which gave women the right to vote, was passed and signed by the governor. In November of the same year, women voted in a general election for the first time, and a large proportion of those eligible registered to vote.

New Zealand thus became the first self-governing country in the world in which women had the vote in national elections. However, women could not yet stand as candidates; that right came only in 1919. Māori women were included in the 1893 law, and many of them took part. The achievement inspired suffragists elsewhere, and in the following decades other countries, such as Australia, Finland and Norway, extended the vote to women. Today, Sheppard's portrait appears on the New Zealand ten-dollar note.

The success of the campaign owed much to Sheppard's organisational skills and her ability to build alliances. She understood that the petitions would impress Parliament only if they were large, orderly and persistent, and she made sure that they were. Historians also point to the particular conditions of a young settler society, in which the traditional political order was less rigid and in which women were valued for their contribution to the economy. These conditions help to explain why the reform came earlier than in older countries, such as Britain, where it was achieved only in 1918 for some women and in 1928 for all.
versions.proof: New Zealand thus became the first self-governing country in the world in which women had the vote in national elections.

text: Heinrich Schliemann was born in 1822 in northern Germany, the son of a poor pastor. According to his own account, he was fascinated as a boy by Homer's epic poems, the Iliad and the Odyssey, and he believed that the city of Troy and the war described in them had been real. He left school early, worked as a grocer's assistant and a clerk, and eventually became a wealthy merchant, partly through trade in Russia and in the California gold rush.

In 1868, having retired from business with a large fortune, Schliemann turned to archaeology. He visited the Turkish coast and became convinced that Troy lay beneath a mound called Hisarlık, in north-western Anatolia, a view that a British expatriate, Frank Calvert, who owned part of the site, had already suggested. Schliemann began to dig there in 1871, and with a great deal of energy and little method, he cut a huge trench through the mound.

The excavations revealed a series of cities built one on top of another. In 1873, Schliemann announced a spectacular discovery: a hoard of gold and silver objects, which he called 'Priam's Treasure', after the legendary king of Troy. He photographed his wife, Sophia, wearing the jewels. The finds made headlines around the world. However, later scholars showed that the treasure was about a thousand years older than the period of the legendary Trojan War, and that the layer Schliemann had identified as Homer's Troy was not the right one.

Schliemann's methods have been widely criticised. His hasty digging destroyed a great deal of evidence, and he was not always honest about his finds; he also smuggled objects out of the Ottoman Empire without permission. Nevertheless, his work revealed that there had been a real, important city at Hisarlık, and later archaeologists, using careful methods, confirmed that it was inhabited for thousands of years. Schliemann also excavated Mycenae in Greece, where he found a gold mask that he believed belonged to the legendary king Agamemnon.

text: After the Second World War, Germany was divided into zones controlled by different countries, and so was its old capital, Berlin, which lay inside the Soviet zone. West Berlin, controlled by the United States, Britain and France, became an island of Western-style freedom, while East Berlin was the capital of communist East Germany. Between 1949 and 1961, about 2.5 million East Germans left for the West, and many of them went through Berlin, because it was the easiest place to cross.

To stop the flow of people, many of whom were young and well educated, the East German government secretly planned to close the border. In the night of 12–13 August 1961, soldiers and workers rolled out barbed wire and began to build a barrier across the city. Families and friends were suddenly separated. The East German government said that the wall protected its country from the West.

Over the years, the barrier was made stronger, and at least 140 people died trying to cross it. By the late 1980s, communist governments in Eastern Europe were becoming weak. On the evening of 9 November 1989, an official announced new travel rules by mistake, and crowds went to the border. The guards opened the gates.

In the night of 12–13 August 1961, soldiers and workers rolled out barbed wire and began to build a barrier across the city. Families and friends were suddenly separated, and the border that had been open for years was closed. The East German authorities called the structure an 'anti-fascist protection wall', claiming that it protected their country from Western aggression.

Over the years, the barrier was strengthened until it consisted of two concrete walls with a 'death strip' between them, which was patrolled by guards and covered with watchtowers, dogs and obstacles. At least 140 people are known to have died trying to cross the wall in or around Berlin, although some historians suggest a higher number. In 1963, the American president John F. By the late 1980s, the communist regimes in Eastern Europe were weakening. In the summer of 1989, Hungary opened its border with Austria, and thousands of East Germans escaped through it. Mass demonstrations in East German cities followed. On the evening of 9 November 1989, an official, answering a question at a press conference, announced that new travel rules would take effect 'immediately', apparently by mistake. Crowds gathered at the checkpoints, and the guards, overwhelmed, opened the gates. Germany was officially reunified on 3 October 1990.
